chapters.title: Why Wanting a Goal Won't Get You There
chapters.hook: Your phone's lock screen shows a finish line you see all day. Your new running shoes still sit in their box by the door.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to pick a big goal and want it badly enough to get there. But a small routine you repeat each day is what brings the result, because winners and losers usually share the very same goal.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you want a result, stop staring at the goal and build the small daily routine that produces it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one result you're after, pick a small step toward it you could repeat daily, and do that step once before dinner tonight.

memorableLines.text: Everyone wants the prize. The daily routine is what wins it.

breakdown.fastRead:
Mateo has paid for a spring ten-kilometre race and told the office he'll run it. His plan is to want it badly enough. Tonight he makes a finish-line photo his lock screen, while his running shoes sit under the bed. His fee and his pride are at stake.

Wanting isn't what he lacks. James Clear, a writer on habits, notes that winners and losers usually share the same goal. What sets winners apart is their system, his word for the small routine they repeat each day. Dave Brailsford showed this as head of British Cycling, a team that had won little. He didn't ask riders to want gold more. He chased tiny gains in everything, from bike seats to riders' pillows to hand washing. About five years later, his riders took 60 percent of the cycling gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. You don't rise to your goal. You fall to the level of your routine.

Keep the goal for direction, but put your effort into the routine. Choose one small step and give it a fixed spot in your day. Mateo keeps the race date, but each morning after his first coffee he runs for ten minutes. Stop staring at the result you want, and build the small daily routine that brings it.
breakdown.deepRead:
Mateo has paid for a spring ten-kilometre race and told the office he'll run it. His plan is to want it badly enough. Tonight he makes a finish-line photo his lock screen, while his running shoes sit under the bed. He'll see that photo dozens of times a day, and nothing else in his day will change. His fee and his pride are at stake.

Wanting isn't what he lacks. James Clear, a writer on habits, points out that winners and losers usually share the same goal. Every runner at the start line hopes for a good time, so the hope can't be what separates them. A reached goal also changes you only for a moment. Clean a messy room once and the goal is met, but the room drifts back unless your daily habits change. What lasts is the system, Clear's word for the small routine you repeat each day. Small routines matter more than they look. Get one percent better each day and in a year you're about 37 times better. Slip one percent a day and you slide toward zero.

Dave Brailsford showed this as head of British Cycling, a team that had won little for a long time. He didn't ask his riders to want gold more. He chased tiny gains in everything they did. The team made bike seats more comfortable, found the best pillows for riders to sleep on and taught them to wash their hands well, so fewer caught colds. No single change was big, but together they added up. About five years later, British riders won 60 percent of the cycling gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Later, British riders won the Tour de France, cycling's most famous race. You don't rise to your goal. You fall to the level of your routine.

So keep the goal as a direction and put your effort into the routine. Ask what small step, done every day, would make the result likely. Then give it a fixed spot in your day, right after something you already do. Mateo keeps the race date. Each morning after his first coffee, he laces up and runs for ten minutes, even when he'd rather not. The lock screen hasn't changed, but his mornings have. Stop staring at the result you want, and build the small daily routine that brings it.
breakdown.fullRead:
Mateo has paid for a spring ten-kilometre race and told the office he'll run it. His plan is to want it badly enough. Tonight he makes a finish-line photo his lock screen, while his running shoes sit under the bed. He'll see that photo dozens of times a day. Nothing else about his day will change. His fee and his pride are at stake.

His plan feels right because wanting is where most people start. You picture the result, pick a date and wait for the drive to carry you. For a week or two, it might. Then comes a cold morning or a late night at work, and the wish gives way. The goal is still there, but nothing in the day was built to reach it.

James Clear, a writer on habits, draws a line between goals and systems. A goal is the result you want. A system is the set of small routines, done day after day, that leads there. Goals are useful for setting a direction. But winners and losers usually share the same goals. Every runner at the start line hopes for a good time, so the hope can't explain who does well. The difference lies in what each one did on ordinary days.

Goals have other weak spots. Reaching one changes you only for a moment. Clean a messy room once and the goal is met, but the room drifts back unless your daily habits change. A goal can also put your happiness on hold. You tell yourself you'll be content once the weight is gone or the job is yours. A routine lets you feel good on every day you keep it.

That is why Clear calls small routines atomic habits. Like an atom, each one is tiny, yet together they hold great power. Their results grow the way interest grows in a savings account. Get one percent better each day and in a year you're about 37 times better. Get one percent worse each day and you slide toward zero. The change on any one day is too small to notice, which makes it easy to dismiss.

Dave Brailsford showed what tiny gains can do. He became head of British Cycling, a team that had won little for a long time. One top bike maker even refused to sell them bikes, worried it would hurt its own sales. Brailsford didn't ask his riders to want gold more. He chased small gains in everything. The team made bike seats more comfortable and found the best pillows for riders to sleep on. A surgeon taught them to wash their hands well, so fewer caught colds. They even painted the inside of the team truck white, so specks of dust would show. About five years later, British riders won 60 percent of the cycling gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Later, British riders won the Tour de France, cycling's most famous race. You don't rise to your goal. You fall to the level of your routine.

So keep the goal as a direction and put your effort into the routine. Ask what small step, done every day, would make the result likely. Give it a fixed spot in your day, right after something you already do. Then expect a slow stretch. Clear calls it the Plateau of Latent Potential, latent meaning hidden. Your work piles up out of sight before the results break through. Many people quit in that flat stretch, which he calls the valley of disappointment. The work was never wasted. It just hadn't shown yet.

Mateo keeps the race date. Each morning after his first coffee, he laces up and runs for ten minutes, even when he'd rather not. The first weeks feel like nothing, and he keeps going anyway. The lock screen hasn't changed, but his mornings have. Stop staring at the result you want, and build the small daily routine that brings it.

examples.title: Flat orders at a small yarn shop
examples.scenario: Khadija sells hand-dyed yarn from her small online shop, and orders have been flat all autumn. On Sunday evening she sits at the kitchen table with a mug of tea and a blank spreadsheet. She means to set a bold target, double her orders by spring, and colour-code a chart for it. Her cursor blinks in the first empty cell.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the spring target as a direction. Then choose one small daily step, like posting one new colour each morning after breakfast.
examples.whyItMatters: Plenty of yarn sellers hope to double their orders. The ones who do put new yarn in front of buyers every single day.

examples.title: A sketchbook stuck at half full
examples.scenario: Nils wanted to fill a whole sketchbook before his birthday. He got himself fired up, spent one Sunday drawing twelve pages, then didn't touch it for a month. The birthday is two weeks away and half the pages are blank. Now the sight of the book on his shelf makes him feel like a fraud, and drawing has stopped being fun.
examples.whatToDo: Stop judging yourself by the birthday deadline. Instead, do one quick sketch every evening after dinner, on whatever page comes next.
examples.whyItMatters: Wanting a full sketchbook never filled a page. A sketch each evening keeps him drawing long after the birthday has passed.

examples.title: A tutor who wants an exam date
examples.scenario: Katja takes Italian with a tutor every Thursday, hoping to chat with her partner's family by summer. She forgets most of each lesson within days. When she suggests ten minutes of practice each day, her tutor waves it off and taps the calendar. "Book the exam for June. Once it's real, you'll find the drive."
examples.whatToDo: Agree to the June date as a direction. Then ask your tutor to set ten minutes of homework for each day, so the routine comes from the lessons too.
examples.whyItMatters: Every learner booked in for June hopes to pass. Ten minutes a day is what keeps the Italian from slipping away between Thursdays.

questions.prompt: Nadia wants to do ten pull-ups by summer. She has fitted a bar in her bedroom doorway and plans to make the number 10 her phone background. She hasn't said when she'll train. What is your best reply?
choices: "Try one or two pull-ups each morning as you pass the bar."
"Look at the number every morning too, so it stays on your mind."
"Write the number on a sticky note by the bar too."
questions.explanation: Nadia has a number to look at but no set time to train. A pull-up or two each morning by the bar builds the strength. Seeing the number more, on a phone or a note, builds none.

questions.prompt: For years, Rustam picked a number of books to read each January and gave up by March. This year he chose the same number, but also began reading ten pages each night after locking the front door. By summer he was well ahead. Why did this year go differently?
choices: His nightly reading added up in a way the number never could.
Setting the same number once again showed how much it meant to him.
Keeping the same number made the aim feel safe and familiar.
questions.explanation: He set the same number that had failed every year, so the number explains nothing new. The ten pages after locking the door were new, and they added up night after night.

questions.prompt: Esteban hopes to pass an accounting exam in the spring. For a month he has studied for fifteen minutes on the train each morning. His office now has him working from home, so the train ride is gone. What should he do?
choices: Use the spare time to aim for a higher mark on the exam.
Do one long study session each weekend instead of the mornings.
Move his study time to just after his first coffee at home.
questions.explanation: The train ride is gone, but the exam is still in spring. Pinning the study to his first coffee keeps it daily. One long weekend session drops the daily habit that has been carrying him.

questions.prompt: Keiko wants a stronger back. She tells you, "I've worked out my routine: ten minutes of stretches. I'll do them on days I feel up to it." What do you tell her?
choices: "Add a clear target too, like touching your toes by spring."
"Tie them to something you already do each day, like your shower."
"Make it a full thirty minutes, so you see a change much sooner."
questions.explanation: Keiko has picked the stretches but left them to her mood, so many days will pass without them. Tying them to her daily shower gives them a fixed spot. A toe-touching target adds another thing to stare at.

questions.prompt: Pablo badly wanted to win best plot at the community garden show. He pinned a photo of the trophy inside his shed and spent the final weekend weeding and planting. The winner, his neighbour, had worked on her plot for twenty minutes every morning since spring. Why did Pablo's plot fall short?
choices: He left his big weekend of weeding and planting until far too late.
He set his sights on a prize far too big for a plot his size.
They both hoped to win, but only she worked on her plot each morning.
questions.explanation: His neighbour wanted the trophy too, so wanting can't explain the gap. Her twenty minutes every morning since spring can. Starting the big weekend earlier would still leave months of daily care missing.

questions.prompt: Helga spent a whole Saturday cleaning her kitchen until it shone. Two weeks later, dishes are piled up and the counters are sticky again. Her parents visit next month. What should she do now?
choices: Tidy up properly whenever the mess gets on her nerves.
Wipe the counters and clear the sink each night after dinner.
Aim for a spotless kitchen by the time her parents visit next month.
questions.explanation: The shining kitchen lasted two weeks, because nothing in her daily routine changed. A wipe and a clear sink every night keeps it clean for good. Tidying only when annoyed lets the mess build back up first.

questions.prompt: A café owner badly hoped for top reviews online. For a month he thought about little else, but changed nothing in how the café ran each day. The reviews stayed mixed. Which of his three thoughts was the trap?
choices: "Aiming for top reviews tells me which way to head."
"Caring this much about top reviews will slowly lift the service."
"The other cafés on this street all hope for top reviews too."
questions.explanation: He changed nothing in how the café ran each day, so caring alone had to lift the service, and it couldn't. Aiming for top reviews did give a direction, and rivals hoping for the same is simply true.

reviewCards.front: Why can't wanting a result badly be what sets winners apart?
reviewCards.back: Because the people who fall short usually wanted the same thing. What differs is the small routine each one kept up, day after day.

reviewCards.front: When a result really matters to you, the first thing to build is ...
reviewCards.back: ... a small step you repeat each day at a fixed point, because the routine, not the wish, produces the result.

reviewCards.front: A man trained hard for months to look fit at his wedding. A year later, he's back where he started. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He treated fitness as a goal to reach, not a routine to keep. Once the wedding passed, nothing in his days kept the change going.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: when you want a result, where should your effort go, and why?
reviewCards.back: Into a small routine you do every day, not into staring at the result, because everyone wants the result and only the routine gets it.

reviewCards.front: You'd like to write a short book this year. So far you have a title and a lot of hope.
reviewCards.back: Keep the book as your direction, pick one small step like fifteen minutes of writing after breakfast, and do it every day.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Turning a result you hope for into one small action you repeat at a set point each day.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down at the start of the week to plan it, I pick one result I'm after and give its small daily step a fixed spot in each day.
When I catch myself daydreaming about a goal instead of doing its daily step, I set the daydream aside and do five minutes of that step right away.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, tie your small daily step to something you already do every day, like your first coffee, and do the step right after that moment once.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, count the days you did your step, not how close the goal looks. If you missed days, shrink the step or move it to a surer spot in your day.

chapters.title: Decide Who You Are Before You Chase a Goal
chapters.hook: You win the thirty-day sugar bet, and next day the break room donuts are back. Your coworker, who never bet, still skips them.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told to pick a big goal and push until you hit it. The trouble is that goals end while your old view of yourself stays, so decide who to become first, then prove it in small ways.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you set a habit goal, decide who you want to become, then prove it with small daily actions.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick who you want to become, then before bed tonight put away one thing on your counter that person would not leave out.

memorableLines.text: Choose who you are becoming, then let each small act count as a vote.

breakdown.fastRead:
Lara gave up sugar for thirty days to win an office bet. On day thirty-one she won and ate three donuts from the break room box, undoing a month of effort. Why does hitting a goal so often end the habit that got you there?

James Clear says most people start at the wrong end. Change has three layers. Outcomes are what you get, processes are what you do, and identity is what you believe about yourself. Lara changed her outcome but still saw herself as someone with a sweet tooth. Clear's fix has two steps. First, decide the type of person you want to be. Then prove it with small wins, since each action is a vote for who you are becoming.

Brian Clark, an entrepreneur, bit his nails all his life until he started paying for manicures. Once his nails looked good, he grew proud of them, and pride stopped the biting. A big goal ends at the finish line and leaves the old you in charge. So Lara asks what kind of person stays off sugar for good. She decides to be someone who eats real food, and each apple she picks over a donut is another vote. A habit outlives the goal once a person decides who to be and proves it in small ways.
breakdown.deepRead:
Lara gave up sugar for thirty days to win an office bet. On day thirty-one she won and ate three donuts from the break room box, undoing a month of effort. She is not unusual. Plenty of people reach a goal and then slide right back. Why does hitting a goal so often end the habit that got you there?

James Clear says most people start at the wrong end. Change has three layers. Outcomes, on the outside, are what you get. Processes, in the middle, are what you do. Identity, at the core, is what you believe about yourself. Lara worked on the outside layer, but in her own mind she still had a sweet tooth. Clear's fix has two steps. First, decide the type of person you want to be. Then prove it to yourself with small wins. Each action is a vote for the person you are becoming. You don't need every vote, just a steady pile of them, so one bad day does not cancel the rest.

Clear tells of Brian Clark, an entrepreneur who had bitten his nails all his life. He began paying for manicures. Once his nails looked good, he grew proud of them, and that pride stopped the biting. Clear also pictures two people turning down a cigarette. One says they are trying to quit. The other says they are not a smoker. The first still sees a smoker who is holding back. The second has already changed who they are.

A big goal feels like the serious choice, so most of us pick a number and push. But a goal ends at the finish line and leaves the old you in charge. Pushing wears out, too, while a habit that is part of who you are needs no push. So Lara asks what kind of person stays off sugar for good. She decides to be someone who eats real food. Each afternoon she walks past the donut box with an apple, and each apple is one more vote. A habit outlives the goal once a person decides who to be and proves it in small ways.
breakdown.fullRead:
Lara gave up sugar for thirty days to win an office bet. On day thirty-one she won and ate three donuts from the break room box, undoing a month of effort. By the next week, the afternoon cookie was back too. She is not unusual. Plenty of people reach a goal and then slide right back to where they started. Why does hitting a goal so often end the habit that got you there?

James Clear says most people start at the wrong end. Change has three layers, like rings around a center. Outcomes, on the outside, are what you get, such as a lower weight or a finished book. Processes, in the middle, are what you do, such as a new routine at the gym. Identity, at the core, is what you believe about yourself. Most people set a goal on the outside and hope the inside follows. Lara worked on the outside layer. In her own mind, she was still someone with a sweet tooth, so when the bet ended, that person took over again.

Clear calls the other approach identity-based habits, meaning habits built around who you want to be rather than what you want to get. The aim shifts. You do not try to run a race. You try to become a runner. You do not try to read one book. You try to become a reader. A goal is something you finish. A way of seeing yourself is something you keep.

Clear's fix has two steps. First, decide the type of person you want to be. A useful question is this: what kind of person could get the result you want? Then prove it to yourself with small wins, again and again. Each action is a vote for the person you are becoming. One vote changes little, and you do not need every one. What matters is a steady pile of votes, so a single bad day does not undo the rest.

Clear tells of Brian Clark, an entrepreneur who had bitten his nails all his life. He began paying for manicures. Once his nails looked good, he grew proud of them, and that pride stopped the biting. His view of himself changed, and the habit followed.

Clear also pictures two people who are offered a cigarette and turn it down. One says they are trying to quit. The other says they are not a smoker. The words are small, but the gap between them is wide. The first person still believes they are a smoker who is holding back. The second has stopped being a smoker in their own mind, so there is nothing left to resist.

This is why the usual advice misleads. A big goal feels like the serious choice, so most of us pick a number and push. But a goal ends at the finish line and leaves the old you in charge. Pushing wears out, too. Once a habit is part of who you are, you stop needing to push yourself to do it. The same pull can work against people. Someone who says they are not a morning person, or are bad at math, tends to act in ways that fit the label. Real change, as Clear sees it, is a change in who you believe you are.

So Lara asks what kind of person stays off sugar for good. She decides to be someone who eats real food. That decision needs proof, so each afternoon she walks past the donut box with an apple. Some days she slips. The pile of apples still grows, and each one is another vote. A habit outlives the goal once a person decides who to be and proves it in small ways.

examples.title: Bedtime ends in shouting again
examples.scenario: Rosa's son, who is six, climbs out of bed for the third time tonight, and once again she hears herself shouting down the hall. She hates the way he flinches at her voice. Afterward she stands at the fridge with a marker, about to write a goal on the calendar: no yelling for thirty days.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the thirty-day count. Decide you are a calm parent at bedtime, then prove it tonight by walking him back to bed in a whisper.
examples.whyItMatters: A count ends on day thirty. Each quiet walk back to bed is a vote for the calm parent she chose.

examples.title: The reading chart after the prize
examples.scenario: Jomo wanted his daughter to win the school reading prize. He taped a chart of twenty books above her desk and set a timer for forty minutes each night. She finished all twenty by March and won. Since then she hasn't opened a book, and yesterday she told her teacher she is just not a reader.
examples.whatToDo: Take down the chart and admit the prize was your goal, not hers. Then ask what she likes to read, and read ten minutes with her tonight.
examples.whyItMatters: The chart ended with the prize and left her calling herself not a reader. Ten easy minutes is a first vote for a new picture.

examples.title: A craft cupboard that won't stay sorted
examples.scenario: Laszlo teaches the four-year-olds at a busy nursery, and his craft cupboard is famous for spilling onto the floor. He decided to be a teacher who keeps an orderly room, and gave up a Saturday to sort every shelf. By Thursday, glue sticks and paint pots were heaped again. He told a colleague he just isn't the tidy type.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the choice to be the orderly teacher, but shrink the proof: before leaving each day, put the paint pots back in one labeled bin.
examples.whyItMatters: One big Saturday was a single vote. A small act every day piles up votes, so the orderly teacher he chose keeps showing up.

questions.prompt: Pedro and Anika both want to stop buying takeout lunches. Pedro sets a goal to save $500 by summer. Anika tells herself she is a person who cooks. Both pack a homemade lunch every weekday. By fall, Pedro has hit his number and is buying takeout again, while Anika still packs lunch. Why did her habit last?
choices: She enjoyed her own cooking more than he enjoyed his.
Each morning she backed up how she had come to see herself.
Without a money target to hit, she felt a lot less pressure.
questions.explanation: Both packed the same lunch every weekday, so the effort was not the difference. Anika had picked who she was, and each lunch backed it up. Pedro's goal ended at $500 and left his old habit in charge.

questions.prompt: Selin has decided she is someone who writes, and she proves it with one page at her kitchen table each morning. This week she is away for work, with meetings from seven every day, though she is up by six. What should she do this week?
choices: Tell herself nightly she's a writer, and write once home.
Type a few lines on her phone each morning before leaving.
Plan to write two full chapters the week after she gets home.
questions.explanation: Meetings from seven leave no room for a full page, but she is up by six, so a few lines on her phone still prove she writes. Telling herself she's a writer without writing casts no vote, and a plan for later starts at the wrong end.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I've decided I'm a runner now. I even changed my profile picture to me in sneakers. I haven't gone out yet, but that's the easy part." What do you say?
choices: "Now back it up with a short jog or two this week."
"Now head out this weekend and run as far as you possibly can."
"Now tell the whole family, so the label sticks."
questions.explanation: Your friend has picked who to be but hasn't gone out once, so nothing backs it up yet. A short jog is a small win that counts as a vote. Telling the family adds more label and no action.

questions.prompt: Erik wanted to stop being late for work. He set a goal of thirty on-time mornings in a row and used three alarms to get up. He made it to thirty, while joking to friends that he's just not a morning person. Two weeks later he is late again. Why did his fix fail?
choices: He fixed the result but still saw himself the old way.
Three alarms were too harsh to rely on for long.
After day thirty he needed a fresh and bigger goal to chase.
questions.explanation: He did reach thirty mornings, so pushing worked while the goal lasted. He still joked he wasn't a morning person, so the finish line left his old self in charge. A bigger goal would end the same way.

questions.prompt: You've chosen to be someone who keeps a tidy home. It's Saturday morning, and a week of clutter fills the living room. What's your first move?
choices: Wait for a quieter weekend, when you have more energy for it.
Spend today clearing every room from top to bottom.
Clear the couch now, then a few more things each day.
questions.explanation: You've already chosen who to be, so what's needed now is proof in small wins. Clearing the couch and a little more each day keeps adding votes. One giant clean is a single effort that ends.

questions.prompt: Shota wants to chat with his wife's parents in Spanish. He set a goal of 1,000 words by May and studied every night. Three weeks in, he missed two nights, fell behind the count, and quit. Which of his three reasons for the plan was the trap?
choices: "My in-laws will be glad when I can talk with them."
"Studying every single night will keep the new words fresh in my head."
"A big number to hit will push me through the hard days."
questions.explanation: Wanting to talk with family and studying daily are both sound. The trap was trusting a big number to push him. Two missed nights put him behind the count, and with no new picture of himself, he quit.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "Starting Monday, I'm hitting the gym five days a week until I've lost twenty pounds. I'll just grind it out." What's the most useful thing to say back?
choices: "Reward yourself with a treat the moment each workout ends."
"Picture who stays healthy for life, and act like that person daily."
"Keep a perfect streak, and restart the whole count any day you slip."
questions.explanation: Your friend is starting with a weight number and plain grit, the outer layer. Picturing a healthy person and acting like one each day starts at the core. A perfect streak turns one missed day into a reason to quit.

reviewCards.front: Each small action you take for a new habit works like ...
reviewCards.back: ... a vote for the person you're becoming. You don't need every vote, only a steady pile of them.

reviewCards.front: Tamika spent a year paying off her credit card, cleared it, then ran it back up within months. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She changed the outcome, a zero balance, but still saw herself as a spender. Once the goal was met, nothing about who she was kept the habit going.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you do before setting a habit goal, and why?
reviewCards.back: Decide who you want to become, then back it up with small actions every day. A goal ends at the finish line, but a new picture of yourself keeps the habit going.

reviewCards.front: You want to be someone who plays guitar, but yours has sat in its case under the bed since spring.
reviewCards.back: Decide you're a guitar player, then prove it today with five minutes of strumming. Repeat it most days, and each session counts as a vote.

reviewCards.front: Why does it help to ask what kind of person would get the result you want, before setting a goal?
reviewCards.back: The question points you at who to become instead of what to get. Then each small action proves it, and the habit lasts past any finish line.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Picking the person you mean to be and backing that choice with small, repeated acts.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking a big goal will finally fix a habit, I ask what kind of person gets that result for good, and do one small thing that person would do.
When I walk in at home and reach for my old evening habit, I stop and do one small thing the person I've decided to be would do instead.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, write one line naming the kind of person you're becoming, then do one small act that backs it up and tick it off.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each evening this week, add a tally mark to a card for every small act that fit the person you chose. On the last day, count the marks and notice the pile, not the misses.

chapters.title: Find the Weak Step in a Habit That Won't Stick
chapters.hook: You're setting tomorrow's alarm for the push-ups you quit last week, promising yourself to want them more. Wanting them was never the problem.
chapters.counterintuition: If a habit keeps slipping, you just need more willpower. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: wanting is only one of the four steps every habit needs. Find the step that's weak and repair that one.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a habit won't stick, find which of its four steps is weak and fix that step.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tell one person today about a habit of yours that keeps fading: which of its four steps is weak, and what you'll change.

memorableLines.text: When a habit fades, look for the broken step before you blame willpower.

breakdown.fastRead:
A fading habit is rarely short on willpower. Usually one of its steps is broken. The psychologist Edward Thorndike put cats in puzzle boxes that opened when a lever was pressed. At first a cat scrambled about until it hit the lever by chance. Over many tries, it learned to press it almost at once. Behavior followed by a satisfying result, he concluded, tends to be repeated.

James Clear breaks every habit into four steps. A cue is the signal that a reward is near, and a craving is the wanting it sparks. The response is what you do, and the reward is the payoff. A fading habit is rarely short on willpower. Usually one of its steps is broken, and no amount of wanting will mend it. That can sound too neat. To see why it holds, it helps to watch a habit being learned from scratch.

The psychologist Edward Thorndike did exactly that with cats. He put each cat in a puzzle box, a closed box with a door that opened when a lever inside was pressed. At first the cat scrambled about, trying one thing after another. Sooner or later it hit the lever by chance, the door opened, and it got out. Thorndike put the cats back in the boxes again and again. Each time they got quicker. In the end a cat pressed the lever almost as soon as it was inside. Behavior followed by a satisfying result, he concluded, tends to be repeated.

The cats needed no extra willpower. Nobody gave them a pep talk. They learned, by trial and error, which action paid off. James Clear starts from this point. A habit, he explains, is a behavior repeated so often that it becomes automatic. Your brain builds it from experience, the same way the cats did. Once built, it works like a mental shortcut. It handles the routine parts of your day, so your mind is free for new problems.

Every habit runs through four steps, always in the same order. The cue is the signal that a reward is near. The craving is the wanting that the cue sparks. The response is what you actually do. The reward is the payoff you were after. Clear splits them into two halves. The cue and the craving are the problem: something catches your notice, and you want a change. The response and the reward are the solution: you act, and you get what you wanted. Think of your phone buzzing on the table. The buzz is the cue. Wanting to know who wrote is the craving. Picking up the phone is the response, and reading the message is the reward.

This is why one weak step matters so much. If any of the four is missing or weak, the habit never forms. With no cue, you never start. With no craving, you don't care enough to act. If the response takes too much effort, you don't do it. With no reward, you have no reason to come back. So Clear gives each step its own law for building a habit. Make the cue obvious. Make the craving attractive. Make the response easy. Make the reward satisfying. To break a bad habit, he turns the four laws around: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult and unsatisfying.

Even so, when a good habit slips, most people reach for willpower and promise to care more. But more wanting leaves a weak cue, a hard response or a missing reward just as weak, and the habit still won't form. A habit that keeps failing is really pointing at the law you need.

Orhan paid for a year of a Spanish app and quit after a week. His first thought was to try harder. Instead he checks the four steps one at a time. He starts with the cue. The app hides on the third screen of his phone, and each morning he opens the news instead. Then the craving: he wants to learn, so that step is fine. The response is easy, since a lesson takes five minutes. The reward works too, because finishing one feels good.

The cue is the weak step, so that is the one he changes. He moves the app to the spot where his thumb lands first each morning. He adds no pep talk and no bigger goal. The lessons come back, and the year he paid for starts to earn its keep. If a habit you want keeps fading, find its weak step and fix that one, and it will hold.

examples.title: A call log too long to keep up
examples.scenario: Deepa sells office printers, and she promised her manager to log every client call the moment she hangs up. She meant it, because good notes help her close deals. But the log is a twelve-box form behind two logins, and by Wednesday she had stopped. Now she holds a sticky note, about to write TRY HARDER across it.
examples.whatToDo: Check each step instead. The doing is the weak one, so jot three lines by the phone after each call and type them in on Friday.
examples.whyItMatters: She already wanted the notes and knew when to write them. The form was too much work, and wanting more can't shrink it.

examples.title: Two-hour study nights after work
examples.scenario: Yusuf takes an online bookkeeping course after work. Each session ends with nothing to show, and the first graded test is two months away. When his study nights slipped, he blamed his drive. He watched pep-talk videos and raised his goal to two hours a night. After a week of midnights, he skipped four nights. Now opening the laptop makes him feel like a failure.
examples.whatToDo: First drop the two-hour goal and go back to short sessions. Then fix the reward: tick a box on a wall calendar after each one.
examples.whyItMatters: More drive only fed the wanting, which was never weak. With no payoff each night, Yusuf had nothing pulling him back to the laptop.

examples.title: Friday night, and the run is tomorrow
examples.scenario: Nomvula and three friends agreed to run together every Saturday, and for two weeks nobody showed up. Each time the plan was just "Saturday morning, near the park." It's now 10 p.m. on Friday, and two friends have already said goodnight in the group chat. The last one awake writes, "We just need to want it more!"
examples.whatToDo: Fix the one step she can tonight: post a set time and corner for the run. Check the other steps together after it.
examples.whyItMatters: A vague plan gave nobody a clear signal to start. A set time and place is a cue that one late message can create.

questions.prompt: You want to drink more water at work. You like it, there's a tap close by, and a full glass feels good. But bottles aren't allowed on desks, so you forget all day. What do you do?
choices: Switch to a flavored water you enjoy more, so you look forward to each glass.
Write down why water matters to your health, and reread it every morning.
Pour a glass each time you pass the kitchen on your way to print.
questions.explanation: You like water, it's close and a glass feels good, so the weak step is the cue, and the bottle ban took it away. A walk you already take puts it back. Flavored water fixes wanting you already have.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I went through all four steps, and the only weak one is the cue. My guitar sits in its case under the bed. Now I'll just remember to get it out." What is your best reply?
choices: Knowing won't do it. Stand the guitar by the sofa where you'll see it.
First check the wanting, the doing and the payoff before moving the guitar.
Good, then aim for a full hour each evening so the habit really sinks in.
questions.explanation: Your friend already found the weak step: the guitar is out of sight. Remembering is just willpower again, so the guitar has to move into view. Checking the other steps repeats work already done.

questions.prompt: Jamal wants to cook dinner instead of ordering in. To fire himself up, he watches cooking videos on the train home. He walks in at seven to an empty fridge and orders anyway. Why didn't the videos help?
choices: The videos showed meals far too fancy for a tired beginner to try at home.
He already wanted to cook, and the empty fridge made it too much work.
Watching on the train left too long a gap before the cooking started.
questions.explanation: Jamal already wanted to cook, so firing up the wanting changed nothing. The empty fridge at seven made the doing too much work, and that step stayed weak. The ride home wasn't what stopped him.

questions.prompt: You want to write in a journal each night. You enjoy it, the notebook sits on your nightstand, and an entry takes five minutes. But afterward nothing feels any different, and you've stopped. What's your next move?
choices: Save your favorite tea for right after each entry, and enjoy it then.
Move the notebook from the nightstand onto your pillow so you can't miss it.
Remind yourself each night how much you wanted this when you began.
questions.explanation: The notebook is in sight, you enjoy writing, and five minutes is easy. What's missing is a payoff after the entry, and tea saved for that moment gives one. Moving the notebook fixes a cue that already works.

questions.prompt: Zeki keeps skipping his evening walk. He gets home at eight and still has dinner to cook. He decides the answer is to push himself harder. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: "If I really wanted it, I'd already be out walking every night."
"My walking shoes sit right by the door, so I can't miss them."
"I enjoy the walk once I'm out, and feel good after."
questions.explanation: His shoes by the door are a real cue, and he does enjoy the walk. The trap was blaming his wanting, when getting home at eight with dinner to cook made the walk too hard to start.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My keyboard has sat boxed in the closet since I moved, and I keep skipping practice. I'll watch concert videos every night to get inspired." What do you say back?
choices: Try the videos for one full week, then unbox the keyboard if that fails.
You want it already. Unbox the keyboard and set it on the desk.
Aim for a full hour each night, so practice really becomes routine.
questions.explanation: Your friend already wants to play, so the videos feed a step that's fine. The boxed keyboard is the weak spot, so it needs to come out now. Waiting a week first just loses that week.

questions.prompt: Arash studies flashcards at the same desk every evening, and he has wanted to pass his licensing exam for years. Still he kept quitting. Then he began adding a gold star to a chart kept inside the flashcard box after each session. He kept going for three months. What made the chart work?
choices: The stars on the chart reminded him each day that the cards were waiting.
The chart made him want to pass the exam more than before.
Each session now ended with something that felt good, which had been missing.
questions.explanation: He already had a set time and place and real wanting. The chart sits inside the box, so it reminds him of nothing. What changed is that each session now ends with a star he enjoys.

reviewCards.front: Bushra wanted to sketch every evening. Her sketchbook stayed shut in a desk drawer, and when she slipped, she vowed to be more disciplined. A week later she had stopped again. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She treated it as a wanting problem. The weak step was the cue: the sketchbook was out of sight. Leaving it open on the table would have repaired that step.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: what do you do when a habit you care about keeps fading?
reviewCards.back: Skip the vow to try harder. Check the cue, the craving, the response and the reward, then repair the one that's failing.

reviewCards.front: You want to stretch each morning. The mat lies by your bed, you enjoy it, and you feel great after. But your routine takes twenty-five minutes, and you keep skipping it. What do you change?
reviewCards.back: The response. Cut the routine to a few minutes you can start at once, since the doing is the only step that's too hard.

reviewCards.front: Why does wanting a habit more rarely save it once it starts fading?
reviewCards.back: Wanting is only one of four steps. If the cue, the effort or the payoff is the weak spot, more wanting leaves that spot just as weak.

reviewCards.front: If a habit has a clear cue, real wanting and an easy action, but you still don't come back to it, the step to repair is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the reward. Give the action a payoff that feels good, so it is worth repeating.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Diagnosing a stalled habit by its cue, craving, response and reward, then repairing the part that fails.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I notice I've skipped a habit I meant to keep, I ask which of the four steps failed and change that one before my next try.
When I finish dinner on Sunday evening, I pick one habit that slipped this week and check its cue, craving, response and reward.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before the day ends, choose one habit that has faded and make one change to its weakest step, such as moving what you need into plain sight.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, take one habit you're building and ask four questions: did you see the cue, want it, find it easy and feel a payoff? Change whichever step got a no.

chapters.title: You Can't Fix a Habit You Don't Notice
chapters.hook: You can name your worst habit in a second. Ask what you did just before it last night, and you'll probably draw a blank.
chapters.counterintuition: The usual advice is to name your bad habit and fight it with willpower. Writing out your whole day and marking each step works better, because the habits you repeat most are the ones you have stopped noticing.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before changing any habit, write down everything you do in a normal day, in order, and mark each one.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write today's actions in order, from waking up until now, mark each good, bad or neutral, and stick the list on your fridge.

memorableLines.text: Your worst habits hide in the ordinary steps you never write down.

breakdown.fastRead:
Dilnoza has a note on her laptop banning TV on weeknights, her third this year. She thinks she knows her bad habit and needs more willpower. Every evening the remote is in her hand before she notices, and her half-sewn dress waits another week. Willpower can't stop what she never sees start.

James Clear says you can't fix what you don't notice. Repeat an action often enough and you stop seeing it, because your brain starts it before you are aware. He tells of a woman who had worked for years as a paramedic. At a family gathering, she said her father-in-law did not look right. She insisted he go to the hospital, where tests found a blocked major artery, and he had surgery. Years of practice trained her to read the signs without thinking. Your habits run on signals you read just as silently.

His tool is the Habits Scorecard, a written list of your actions in a normal day, in order. Mark each action good, bad or neutral, by whether it moves you toward the person you want to be. Dilnoza's list shows the TV starts when she drops onto the sofa to pull off her boots. Write out a normal day and mark each step, and you will see what to change before you try.

Each lost evening makes her trust her own promises a little less.

Willpower needs a moment of choice, a point where she stops and decides. She never sees that moment arrive. By the time she thinks about the TV, it is already on. And calling it too much TV is only a label. It tells her what the habit is called, not how it starts.

James Clear says you can't change a habit until you notice it. That sounds obvious, but there is a catch. The more often you repeat an action, the less you see it. At first a new action takes effort and attention. Repeat it enough times and your brain takes over. It spots the signal and starts the habit before you are aware, so the habits you do most are the ones you notice least.

He tells of a woman who had worked for years as a paramedic. At a family gathering, she looked at her father-in-law and said he did not look right. He felt fine. So the first step is to drag your habits back into view. Clear's tool for this is the Habits Scorecard. Write down everything you do in a normal day, in order, starting when you wake up. Bad means it pulls you away from that person, and neutral means it does neither. The same action can earn different marks for different people, because it depends on who each person wants to become. Before you act, say out loud what you are about to do and what will follow from it.

Dilnoza tries the scorecard on a Tuesday. Her list reads like a diary of small moves. She puts her keys in the bowl and marks it neutral. She drops onto the sofa to pull off her boots, also neutral. Then she picks up the remote, and that one is bad. On paper she sees that the TV never starts with a choice to watch. It starts the moment she sits down on the sofa, a step she had never counted as part of the habit. Now she knows where her evenings really turn. Write out a normal day and mark each step, and you will see what to change before you try.

examples.title: Dry beds in the community garden
examples.scenario: Carlos promised the neighbours in his community garden group that he would water the shared beds before work each morning. Three weeks in, the beds are dry and someone has taped a polite note to the gate. Carlos is sure the problem is laziness. On Sunday night he sits at the kitchen table, pen in hand, about to write himself a stricter promise.
examples.whatToDo: Before promising anything, write out a normal weekday morning, every step from the alarm to the front door, and mark each one good, bad or neutral.
examples.whyItMatters: His mornings run on autopilot, so he can't see where the watering slips away. The list shows him what really happens.

examples.title: Late again at the flower shop
examples.scenario: Gabriela opens the flower shop at eight, and she has been late four times this month. Sure it was weak willpower, she told her manager it would never happen again. Two days later she was ten minutes late, with customers waiting at the locked door. Now her manager has stopped believing her promises, and Gabriela still can't say where her mornings go.
examples.whatToDo: Tell your manager the promise didn't work, then write out a normal morning in order and mark each step before promising anything new.
examples.whyItMatters: Willpower failed because her late start began before she noticed it. The list shows her those hidden steps.

examples.title: The list with the games left out
examples.scenario: Chidi failed his first statistics exam at college and wants to change how he studies. He wrote out a normal day and marked each step. The list looks tidy: lectures, library, dinner. It leaves out the two hours of video games he plays in his room after dinner, because seeing them in ink makes him cringe. So the list shows him nothing to fix.
examples.whatToDo: Add every missing step, the games included, and mark each one by the student you want to become, not by what it says about you.
examples.whyItMatters: The steps he hides are the ones he most needs to see. Marking the action, without blame, makes them easier to write down.

questions.prompt: Your friend Sven says, "I've written my two bad habits on a card: snacking late at night and skipping my run. Now it's just willpower." What's your best reply?
choices: "Write out your whole day in order and mark each step, not only those two."
"Write down every time those two happen this week, and mark which one costs you more."
"Write a plan to drop one of them, and mark the day you start."
questions.explanation: Sven's card holds only the two habits, so it can't show what sets them off. A whole day written in order and marked shows the steps before them. Counting how often they happen still hides those steps.

questions.prompt: Mehmet wanted to stop buying a pastry on his walk to work. Each morning he told himself to be strong. Most days he only noticed the paper bag once he was at his desk. Why did being strong fail him?
choices: He didn't really care enough about stopping to turn the pastry down on busy mornings.
The habit ran before he was aware, so he had no moment to resist.
He hadn't decided clearly enough that the pastry was doing him harm.
questions.explanation: Mehmet only saw the bag at his desk, so the habit ran before he was aware. Being strong needs a moment he never saw. Caring more can't help in a moment that never arrives.

questions.prompt: Ayesha keeps arriving late and flustered to her Tuesday evening pottery class, though she leaves work on time. What should she do first?
choices: Write down everything she does on a Tuesday, from waking up, and mark each step.
Write down her last few late arrivals and mark the excuse she gave for each one.
Write a firm rule in her diary and mark every Tuesday she keeps it.
questions.explanation: Ayesha leaves work on time, so the lost minutes hide in steps she isn't seeing. Writing out her whole Tuesday shows them. Her old excuses only repeat what she already believes happened.

questions.prompt: Olumide set out to cut down on coffee by willpower alone, for three reasons. Weeks later he writes out a normal day and counts five cups, not the two he thought. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: "Coffee is the habit I most want to change."
"I already know when and why I reach for coffee."
"Drinking less coffee after lunch would help me sleep a lot better."
questions.explanation: He found five cups, not two, so he didn't know his habit as well as he thought. Choosing coffee first and hoping for better sleep were fair reasons. Trusting what he thought he knew was the trap.

questions.prompt: On Friday, your friend Jana says, "I snap at my team most mornings. I know it's a bad habit, so from Monday I'll just stop myself." What do you tell her?
choices: "Start on Monday, and if it slips, write down how that morning went."
"Ask your team to write down each time you snap, so you can see it."
"Before Monday, write down a whole morning, step by step, and rate each one."
questions.explanation: Jana starts Monday, so the weekend gives her time to write out a morning first and see what leads to the snapping. Her team's notes would show only the snaps, not the steps before them.

questions.prompt: Thandi meant to practise her trumpet after work but rarely did, however hard she tried. Then she wrote out a normal weekday in order and marked each step. She was surprised to find every evening began with lying on her bed in her work clothes. She changed that step and now practises most days. Why did the list help where trying hard hadn't?
choices: It showed her a step she had been doing without noticing it.
Seeing each step on paper made her guilty enough to push herself harder.
Each bad step gave her a score to beat next week.
questions.explanation: Thandi was surprised by how her evenings began, so the list showed her a step she did without noticing. Trying hard couldn't reach it. Guilt about the list wouldn't have shown her which step to change.

questions.prompt: You're writing out a normal day and reach a line you can't mark: two hours of chess puzzles on your laptop each evening. You want to be someone who sleeps by eleven, and the puzzles run past midnight. How should that line be marked?
choices: Mark it neutral, since those two hours do no clear harm.
Mark it good, since those two hours are the best part of your day.
Mark it by the person those two hours are turning you into.
questions.explanation: You want to sleep by eleven and the puzzles run past midnight, so measured against the person you want to be, the line is bad. Calling it harmless, or the best part of the day, skips that test.

reviewCards.front: Before you try to change a habit, what's the first thing to do, and why?
reviewCards.back: Write down everything you do in a normal day, in order, and mark each step good, bad or neutral, because the habits you repeat most are the ones you stop seeing.

reviewCards.front: You keep ending up in a fast-food queue on your drive home, and you've vowed to be stronger next week.
reviewCards.back: Before next week, write out a normal day, the drive home included, and mark each step, so you see what leads you into the queue.

reviewCards.front: Why can't willpower alone stop a habit you've done for years?
reviewCards.back: The more you repeat it, the less you see it. Your brain starts it before you're aware, so there's no moment for willpower to step in.

reviewCards.front: Each action on your list gets marked good, bad or neutral according to ...
reviewCards.back: ... whether it moves you toward the person you want to be, pulls you away, or does neither.

reviewCards.front: A friend wanted to stop shouting at the TV during football matches. He told himself he knew exactly why he did it and resolved to stay calm. Nothing changed. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He trusted that he already knew his habit and leaned on willpower. Writing out a normal match night, step by step and marked, would have shown what sets the shouting off.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Seeing your own routine clearly on paper before you try to change any part of it.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down after getting home from work or class, I write down what I did since waking, in order, and mark each step good, bad or neutral.
When I catch myself thinking I just need more willpower to stop, I write out a normal day around that habit, in order, and mark each step before trying anything else.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next 24 hours, keep a running list and add each action as you do it. Before you sleep, mark every line good, bad or neutral.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: On two normal days this week, write out every step in order and mark each one. At the weekend, compare the lists and look for the steps that come just before each bad mark.

chapters.title: Give Every New Habit a Time and a Place
chapters.hook: You tell yourself you'll start once the right moment comes. It rarely does, and the pool card you paid for stays in its paper sleeve.
chapters.counterintuition: We tend to think a new habit starts once we want it badly enough. What works is writing down the exact time and place for it, since a set plan removes the daily choice about whether to act.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you start a new habit, write down the exact time and place you will do it.
chapters.tryThisNow: Right now, write one line for a habit you keep putting off, naming what you'll do, the exact time and the place.

memorableLines.text: A habit you only want waits; a habit with a time and place happens.

breakdown.fastRead:
Salma and her brother Dawit joined the same pool on the same day. Three months later, Dawit swims every Tuesday and Thursday, and Salma has not been once. She still pays the monthly fee for a card in its paper sleeve. Why does one show up while the other, just as keen, never starts?

James Clear says the gap is rarely desire. It is a plan. Researchers in Britain split people who wanted to exercise more into three groups. All of them tracked their workouts. One group also read about how exercise helps the heart. The third did both and wrote down the day, time and place they would exercise that week. examples.title: The hybrid manual above the parts counter
examples.scenario: Matias runs a two-bay car repair shop. A thick manual on hybrid engines has sat on the shelf above the parts counter since spring, and last week he turned away two hybrid jobs. He keeps telling himself he'll read it when the shop goes quiet. It's 7:20 a.m., the roller door is still down, and he lifts the manual off the shelf.
examples.whatToDo: Write on the cover: ten pages at 7:20 each weekday, on the stool by the parts counter, before the roller door goes up.
examples.whyItMatters: A garage rarely goes quiet. With the hour and the stool fixed, he stops deciding each morning whether to read.

examples.title: Six budget videos and an overdraft fee
examples.scenario: Yasmin wanted to start checking her spending once a week. Instead of picking a day, she paid for a budgeting app and saved six videos on why tracking money matters, waiting to feel ready. A month on, she has opened the app once. This morning her bank charged her a $30 overdraft fee for a gym payment she forgot.
examples.whatToDo: Skip the next video. Write one line now: every Sunday at 9 a.m., on the living-room sofa, she checks the week's spending in her bank app.
examples.whyItMatters: More reasons barely helped the British exercisers who read them. What she lacked was a set slot, not a stronger wish to save.

examples.title: A friend who laughs at the library timetable
examples.scenario: Nkechi, fifteen, has a chemistry test in a month and wants to do ten practice questions every school day. In her planner she wrote: 4 p.m., the library table by the window. Today her friend Piotr drops into the seat across from her. "Nobody needs a timetable," he says. "Just study when you feel like it. Come out to the bench with us."
examples.whatToDo: Keep the plan exact, but tie it to a step Piotr isn't part of: straight after she steps off the bus home, ten questions at her bedroom desk.
examples.whyItMatters: Stepping off the bus happens every school day, and one action tends to set off the next, so the questions no longer hang on Piotr.

questions.prompt: Jabari wants to start doing push-ups each evening. He taped five reasons to his bathroom mirror and promised to do them once he felt up to it. Two weeks later he has done them twice. Why didn't the reasons help?
choices: Five reasons were too few to keep him eager.
Nothing said which hour and which room the push-ups belonged to.
The bathroom mirror was a poor spot for reasons needed at night.
questions.explanation: He promised to do them once he felt up to it, so no evening had a set hour or room. Extra reasons barely helped the British readers either. A fixed slot would have ended the daily choice.

questions.prompt: You've just bought floss and want to start using it every night. You get home at different hours, but you brush your teeth at 10:30 each night. What's your first move?
choices: Start by flossing both morning and night, so the habit builds twice as fast.
Floss at 10:30 on the nights you still have energy left.
Note on your phone: floss at 10:30 each night, at the bathroom sink.
questions.explanation: You brush at 10:30 every night, so a note naming that hour and the sink gives flossing a fixed slot. Adding an energy check brings back the daily choice of whether to floss.

questions.prompt: Xiomara decided to start writing one page of her novel a day, without choosing when she'd write. A month later she has two pages. Which of her three reasons was the trap?
choices: One page is short enough to finish even on a long workday.
If she wants it enough, a free hour will turn up.
She has finished short stories before, so she can write.
questions.explanation: A page is small, and her stories show she can write. The trap was trusting a free hour to turn up. With none chosen, she waited each day, and the hour rarely came.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm finally learning to code. I want it badly, so I'll do it on whichever evenings turn out quiet." What is your best reply?
choices: "Choose which evenings and which desk now, and put them in your calendar."
"Wait for the first quiet evening, then pick a schedule from there."
"Set a start date, like next Monday, so you know just when to begin."
questions.explanation: Your friend is counting on quiet evenings to turn up. Choosing the evenings and the desk now leaves none of them to chance. A start date fixes only the first day, not the rest.

questions.prompt: For months, a bus driver meant to do ten minutes of sign language a day, whenever his shifts allowed. Last Sunday he wrote in his diary: 5 p.m., the depot break room where he has eaten lunch for years. He has practised every day since. Why did the diary line work?
choices: It fixed the moment in advance, so no daily choice was left.
Writing it in the diary made him care more about learning.
The break room is quiet, which makes it easy to focus in there.
questions.explanation: The break room had been quiet for years, and his wish was the same as before. What changed was a fixed hour and room, which ended the daily choice of whether to practise.

questions.prompt: For a month you've done ten chess puzzles each weeknight at 7, at your desk. From Monday, your new job keeps you at work until 8. What do you do now?
choices: Pause the puzzles until the new job settles, then choose a fresh hour.
Fit the puzzles into free gaps the new job leaves.
Choose now which new hour and seat the puzzles will get.
questions.explanation: From Monday the 7 o'clock slot is gone, so choosing its replacement now keeps a set hour and seat. Pausing, or squeezing puzzles into free gaps, leaves them waiting for a moment that rarely comes.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "My sticky note says harmonica at 6:30 every morning. Where I play can change from day to day, so the hard part's done." What do you tell your friend?
choices: "Tick each morning on the note, so you see your streak."
"Add which room it happens in, so each morning is fully settled."
"Move it to 6 instead, so nothing else in the morning can crowd it."
questions.explanation: Your friend has the hour but says the place can change each day, so half the plan is still open. Naming the room settles it. A streak tally says nothing about where to play.

reviewCards.back: Her note named the habit but not when or where. With no set hour or room, each day she still had to decide whether to play, and the free moment rarely came.

reviewCards.back: Give it a written time and place, so you stop waiting to feel ready and just follow what you already decided.

When I catch myself thinking I'll start once things calm down, I pick an exact time and place for that habit and write them down at once.

chapters.title: What You See Decides What You Do
chapters.hook: The jump rope you swore you'd use is coiled in a drawer. Your willpower isn't the problem. The drawer is.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think eating better or practicing more comes down to trying harder and staying motivated. Actually, what you see around you steers you more, because every habit starts with a cue, a signal to act, and sight is your strongest sense.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Put the thing you need for a good habit where your eyes land on it every day.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one good habit and, before bed tonight, move the thing it needs to the spot your eyes land on first each morning.

memorableLines.text: Your eyes start your habits, so give them something good to find.

breakdown.fastRead:
What sits in front of your eyes shapes your habits more than how badly you want them. Anne Thorndike, a doctor at Massachusetts General Hospital, showed this in its cafeteria. Without saying a word, she put bottled water in the fridges by the registers and in baskets around the room. Over three months, soda sales fell and water sales rose by 25.8 percent. Nobody was told to drink better. People just saw water first.

James Clear explains why. Every habit starts with a cue, a signal to act, and sight is your strongest sense. Change what you see, and you change what you do. You rarely notice this pull, so when a habit slips, you blame your willpower and promise to try harder.

Mirela bought a jump rope to get fit for a June hike. It sits in a drawer while she vows to find more drive. The fix has three steps. Pick the habit, find the one thing it needs, and put that thing where your eyes land when you could act. She hangs the rope by her front door, beside her keys. That evening she sees it as she walks in, and jumps for ten minutes with her coat still on. Stop leaning on drive, and keep what a habit needs where you see it daily.
