examples.title: The Friday question about call notes
examples.scenario: Monika sells gym equipment to hotels. Three weeks ago she started typing her call notes right after each call, not at six o'clock. In Friday's team huddle, her lead asks if the new routine has stuck yet. Monika has her answer ready: three weeks down, one to go, and then it will run on its own. She opens her mouth to say it.
examples.whatToDo: Answer with how many calls she has actually written up right away, and judge the routine by that number, not by the weeks.
examples.whyItMatters: Each write-up made the next one take less thought. Her count of write-ups, not three weeks on the calendar, shows how close she is.

examples.title: Free throws after the thirty-day chart
examples.scenario: Amina, fifteen, wanted shooting free throws at lunch to become automatic, so she taped a thirty-day chart inside her school planner. Each day she crossed off a box, whether she shot or not. On day thirty she told her coach the habit was built. Two weeks later she sits on the bleachers most lunches, and her coach has stopped saving her a ball.
examples.whatToDo: Tell the coach the chart counted days, not lunches on the court. Then tally the lunches she really shot and fit in more from there.
examples.whyItMatters: Crossing off days built nothing. Only the lunches she actually shot made shooting take less thought, so that number is where she really stands.

examples.title: A push-up pact on twelve-hour shifts
examples.scenario: Karim and three friends made a pact: each picks a habit and reports on a Sunday video call. Karim chose twenty push-ups a day. Then the bakery put him on twelve-hour shifts, and this week he managed only two days, both near midnight. On Sunday a friend says, 'Maybe wait until your shifts calm down.' Karim feels like the weak link.
examples.whatToDo: Shrink it to five push-ups he can do in under a minute, fit a set into every break, and count each set.
examples.whyItMatters: Two long sessions a week give him two repeats. Several short sets a day give him dozens, and repeats are what build the habit.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I tick a box each evening I write my 100 words for my novel. Twelve ticks so far. Two more weeks and the month is up, and then it's a habit." What is your best reply?
choices: "Spend those two weeks planning the plot, so every writing evening goes much further."
"Keep ticking, but stop waiting on the calendar and write on more evenings."
"Keep ticking, and also note the minutes each evening's writing session takes."
questions.explanation: Your friend counts the evenings, which is the useful part, but is waiting for the month to finish the job. More writing evenings mean more repeats. Planning the plot or timing sessions leaves your friend still waiting on the calendar.

questions.prompt: Ilse joined a thirty-day challenge to cycle to work. She rode on eight of the thirty days, called the habit done on day 31, and is back on the bus every day. Why didn't her month build the habit?
choices: A month was just too short for something as hard as daily cycling.
She didn't want it badly enough to push through hard mornings.
Her rides were far too few for cycling to feel automatic yet.
questions.explanation: Ilse rode only eight times in the month. Habits grow from repeats, not from days on a calendar, so eight rides left cycling far from running by itself. A longer month with the same few rides would not help.

questions.prompt: Three weeks ago you started a sign language course at home. Some nights you work through a lesson, and some you skip. You want to judge how close it is to running on its own. What is your first step?
choices: Tally up the evenings you really sat down and practised signing.
Work out the weeks still left until a full month.
Write down why learning sign language matters to you, then reread it.
questions.explanation: You skip some nights, so three weeks on the calendar tells you little. Each session you actually practise makes the next take less thought, so the tally shows where you stand. Rereading your reasons adds no sessions.

questions.prompt: Felipe set out to clear his desk at the end of each workday, telling himself three things as he went. He cleared it on nine of the first thirty days, stopped keeping an eye on it after day 30, and the clutter is back. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: Each clear-up should feel a little easier than the one just before it.
Once a month has passed, clearing up will run on its own.
Clearing up after more workdays will help it stick much sooner.
questions.explanation: Felipe cleared his desk only nine times, then stopped watching it because the month was up. The month built nothing on its own; the nine clear-ups did. His other two thoughts fit how repeats build a habit.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm taking up skateboarding. I'll go to the skate park on Saturdays for a month, and if it doesn't feel natural by then, I'll sell the board." What do you say?
choices: "Four Saturdays is only four rides, so add short rides on weekday evenings."
"First spend a week planning which tricks to learn, then head out."
"Keep to Saturdays, but bring a friend along so the month is more fun."
questions.explanation: Saturdays for a month means only four rides, too few for skating to feel natural. Weekday rides add repeats. Planning tricks first is motion, which adds no rides, and a friend along still leaves just four.

questions.prompt: Aylin and a coworker began taking the stairs at their office on the same Monday. He climbs all the way up once each morning. She takes the stairs whenever she changes floors, about six short climbs a day. A month later she heads for the stairs without thinking, but he still has to talk himself into it. What made the difference for her?
choices: She cared more about it, so she put more effort into every single climb.
Her climbs added up to more minutes on the stairs than his.
She climbed far more often, so the stairs got easier to choose sooner.
questions.explanation: Both started the same Monday. She climbed about six times a day to his once, and each climb made the next easier. Minutes don't build a habit; the number of climbs does.

questions.prompt: You've been tallying your morning writing sessions, twenty-two so far. Now a new job starts, and for the next month your mornings are gone and your days are packed. How do you keep the habit growing?
choices: Write a few lines each lunch break, and add each one to the tally.
Pause the tally this month and pick it up once mornings return.
Save it all for one long writing session each Sunday, and tally only that.
questions.explanation: With your mornings gone, the habit needs a smaller piece that fits your days. A few lines at lunch adds a repeat every day. One Sunday session adds one a week, and a pause adds none.

reviewCards.front: Why can a habit you've had for three months still feel like hard work?
reviewCards.back: Because habits grow from repeats, not from time. If you only did it a handful of times in those months, it hasn't had enough repeats to run on its own.

reviewCards.front: To tell how close a new habit is to running by itself, check ...
reviewCards.back: ... how many times you've actually done it, not how long ago you began.

reviewCards.front: A man circled day 30 on his calendar for a new touch-typing practice. He practised about once a week, and on day 30 he still had to drag himself to the keyboard. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He judged by the calendar. Four or so sessions are too few repeats; he needed to practise more often, not wait out more days.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: what should you keep track of when you start a new habit, and why?
reviewCards.back: The number of times you actually do it, not the days since you started. Each repeat makes the next one easier, so the count shows how close you are.

reviewCards.front: Five weeks ago you began packing your bag for the next day each night, but you've done it only seven times. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Stop judging it by the five weeks. Seven is your real count, so look for ways to fit it into more of your nights.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Measuring a new habit by how often you've actually done it, then making room for more goes.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself saying how many days or weeks I've kept a habit, I work out how many times I actually did it and use that number instead.
When I finish the last workday of my week, I tally how many times I did my new habit that week and pick one more spot to fit in a repeat.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Tonight, write down how many times you have actually done your newest habit since you began, then pick one extra moment in your day to fit in another repeat.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, compare your count of repeats with the week before. If it held steady or dropped, find one more short spot in your day to do the habit.

chapters.title: Make Your Skipped Habits Easier to Start
chapters.hook: The healthy lunch you meant to pack gets skipped. The phone you never meant to check gets checked all morning.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think skipping a habit they care about means they lack willpower. Actually, the habit usually takes too many steps to start, because people drift toward whatever takes the least work.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a good habit keeps slipping, cut the steps between you and starting it instead of pushing harder.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write down every step it takes to start one habit you keep skipping, do one ahead tonight, and leave the list where it happens.

memorableLines.text: A habit you skip needs fewer steps in front of it, not more grit.

breakdown.fastRead:
Skipping a habit you care about rarely means you care too little. Usually the habit takes too many steps to start. James Clear calls this the Law of Least Effort: people drift toward whatever takes the least work. Clear shows this pull with an idea from the writer Jared Diamond. Diamond noticed that Eurasia stretches east to west, while the Americas run north to south. Crops moving across Eurasia met the same kind of weather, so they spread fast. In the Americas, moving north or south meant new weather, and crops spread slowly. Less in the way meant faster spread.

Willpower gets the blame because you see the moment you quit, not the chores before it. Samira wants to bring lunch to work and save for a trip. Each morning she must find a box, hunt for its lid and cook something. By the 7:40 bus she gives up and buys a sandwich.

So she lists each step and cuts what she can. After dinner, she gets ready ahead of time, spooning leftovers into a box and setting it at the front of the fridge. Now mornings take one step, and she grabs the box on her way out. Good habits stick when the steps in front of them are cut, not when people push harder.

breakdown.fullRead:
Skipping a habit you care about rarely means you care too little. Usually the habit takes too many steps to start. James Clear calls this the Law of Least Effort. People drift toward whatever takes the least work, and the more energy a habit takes, the less likely it is to happen. This is not a flaw in a few weak people. It is how everyone works. Picking up your phone takes one move. A good habit may hide several small chores before it even begins, and each one is a chance to stop.

Clear shows this pull with an idea from the writer Jared Diamond. Diamond noticed that Eurasia stretches east to west, while the Americas run north to south. Crops moving east or west across Eurasia met much the same weather, so farmers far along could grow them too. In the Americas, moving a crop north or south meant new weather at every stage, and crops spread slowly. Nobody in Eurasia had to push the crops harder. There was simply less in the way, and less in the way meant faster spread.

Japanese factories turned the same idea into a way of working. They hunted for every wasted step in how they made things and took it out. Clear calls this addition by subtraction, which means getting more of what you want by taking things away. A habit works the same way. The quickest route to doing it more often is rarely to add effort. It is to remove the hassle between you and the first move.

Even so, willpower gets the blame when a habit slips. You see the moment you quit, and it feels like a choice you made badly. You don't see the chores before it, because each one is small. Finding a lid takes a minute. Looking for a charger takes another. On their own they seem harmless. Together they decide whether the habit happens, and scolding yourself removes none of them.

Samira wants to bring lunch to work. She is saving for a trip, and every bought lunch eats into it. Each morning she must find a box, hunt for its lid and cook something before the 7:40 bus. Most days she gives up and buys a sandwich at the station. She tells herself she is lazy. She isn't. Her habit starts with three chores, and the sandwich starts with none.

So she works through it in order. First she lists each step between waking up and having lunch in her bag. Next she cuts what she can, keeping one box with its lid already on at the front of one cupboard. Then she gets the rest ready ahead of time. After dinner, she spoons leftovers into the box and sets it at the front of the fridge. Clear's advice is to leave your space ready for the next time you need it, so each start is easy.

Now mornings take one step. She opens the fridge, grabs the box and heads for the bus. She has not become tougher. Her mornings simply have less in the way. Clear also runs the idea in reverse, adding steps in front of a habit you want less of so it happens less. For a good habit that keeps slipping, the work goes the other way. Good habits stick when the steps in front of them are cut, not when people push harder.

examples.title: Sunday litter-pick, missed again
examples.scenario: Ibrahim signed up for his street's Sunday morning litter-pick, and he has missed three of the last four. Each time, he had to dig his gloves out of the shed, find bin bags in a kitchen drawer and borrow a grabber from next door. The neighbours have started asking where he is. On Saturday night he picks up his phone to set a louder alarm.
examples.whatToDo: Put the gloves and bin bags in one bag beside your shoes tonight, and borrow the grabber this evening too.
examples.whyItMatters: He cares about the street. Three hunts stand between him and the door, and people drift toward whatever takes the least work.

examples.title: Late nights at the shoe-repair shop
examples.scenario: Ahmed runs a small shoe-repair shop and wants to log each day's jobs in his order book before closing. He kept forgetting, so he made himself a rule: no going home until it's done. Now he stays late most nights, grumbling, and has missed dinner with his family twice. The book still lives in a back-room drawer under boxes of laces.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the stay-late rule, then move the order book and a pen beside the till, so logging a job takes one step.
examples.whyItMatters: Staying late added pain but no help. The book under the laces was the hold-up, and fewer steps make a habit more likely.

examples.title: A textbook she can't face
examples.scenario: Freya is an apprentice electrician with a written exam in six weeks. She has already moved her textbook from her workshop locker to the small table beside her armchair. Still, each evening she walks past it. Opening it means finding her place and choosing what to study, and the fear of how much she doesn't know makes her stomach drop.
examples.whatToDo: Before bed, open the book at the next page to study, mark one question and lay a pencil across it.
examples.whyItMatters: Her fear strikes at finding her place. Getting the book ready ahead of time leaves only one small step between her and starting.

questions.prompt: A man wants to do sit-ups every morning. His mat is rolled up behind the vacuum cleaner in the hall cupboard. He vows to be tougher and sets an early alarm, yet still skips most mornings. Why did his vow fail?
choices: Waking so early left him too sleepy for sit-ups.
His vow had no penalty, so skipping it cost him nothing.
His vow left getting started just as slow as before.
questions.explanation: The mat stayed behind the vacuum cleaner, so every morning began with a chore. Being tougher changed none of that. A penalty would only add pressure to the same slow start.

questions.prompt: You mean to practise ukulele every evening. It sits in its case on top of the wardrobe, and you need a chair to reach it. You've skipped four nights. What do you do?
choices: Take it down tonight and leave it out in the living room.
Practise mornings instead, when fetching the chair feels less tiring.
Leave a chair beside the wardrobe so the case is easier to reach.
questions.explanation: The case sits on the wardrobe, so each evening starts with a chair and a climb. Leaving it out in the living room removes those steps. A chair by the wardrobe still leaves the climb.

questions.prompt: A woman keeps skipping her Wednesday dance class. Her dance shoes end up in the laundry basket upstairs each week, so she hunts for them after work. She tells herself three things about it, decides to be tougher, and skips again. Which of her three reasons was the trap?
choices: "I enjoy the class once I get there."
"I keep skipping, so I can't want it enough."
"Hunting for my dance shoes after work takes so long."
questions.explanation: Her shoes end up in a basket upstairs, so every Wednesday starts with a hunt. That hunt is the real snag. Deciding she didn't want it enough hid the one thing she could fix.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I keep skipping my Sunday letter to my gran. The writing paper's always lost and I never have stamps. This week I'll just make myself do it." What is your best reply?
choices: "Write to her tonight, while you still feel cross with yourself."
"Jot down things to tell her during the week, so you have news."
"Get what you need and keep it where you write on Sundays."
questions.explanation: The paper is lost and there are no stamps, so every Sunday starts with a hunt. Keeping what the letter needs where your friend writes ends it. Writing tonight in a cross mood leaves the hunt in place.

questions.prompt: A woman wanted to practise calligraphy each night but rarely did. Her pen and ink sat in plain sight on a shelf, yet she had to clear the table, fetch the ink down and fill her pen. Now she leaves the pen filled and paper out on a side desk. She practises most nights. Why did this work?
choices: Seeing the pen each night kept reminding her she cared.
Starting now takes one move instead of three small chores first.
Setting things out the night before made her feel far more determined.
questions.explanation: Her pen was in plain sight all along, so seeing it wasn't new. What changed was the start: no clearing, fetching or filling, only one move. Her feelings weren't what changed.

questions.prompt: You want to play violin each evening. Your partner wants the living room tidy, so the case can't stay out there. Your bedroom has an empty shelf. How do you set it up?
choices: Keep it tuned, with the case open, on the bedroom shelf.
Leave it out in the living room anyway; it's your home too.
Shelve the case in the bedroom and play only weekends.
questions.explanation: The living room must stay tidy, but the bedroom shelf is free. A tuned violin in an open case there still takes one move to start. Playing only at weekends drops the evenings you wanted.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I worked out why I never sort my photos on Sundays. The laptop's in a cupboard, the hard drive is in a box and the cable's somewhere in the car. I've listed it all, so I'm fine now." What do you tell your friend?
choices: "Pin the list up where you'll see it each Sunday."
"Now put every item on that list together in one drawer."
"Make the list longer still, so that no small hold-up is missed."
questions.explanation: Listing the hold-ups only names them. The laptop, drive and cable still sit in three places, so Sunday still starts with a hunt. Putting them together removes it; pinning up the list does not.

reviewCards.front: When a habit you care about keeps getting skipped, the first thing to look at is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the small steps between you and starting it, so you can remove or get ready ahead as many of them as you can.

reviewCards.front: A man meant to wash his car every Saturday. The bucket was in the shed, the sponge under the sink and the soap upstairs. He called himself lazy, promised to try harder, and still skipped. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He blamed his will when the real snag was a hunt in three places. Keeping the bucket, sponge and soap together would have made starting easy.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: what do you do when a good habit keeps slipping, and why?
reviewCards.back: Remove the chores that stand before it instead of pushing harder, because people drift toward whatever takes the least work.

reviewCards.front: You want to cook porridge before work, but the pot is usually in the sink and the oats are on a high shelf.
reviewCards.back: The night before, wash the pot, set it on the stove and leave the oats beside it, so the morning starts in one move.

reviewCards.front: Why does making a habit easier to start work better than wanting it more?
reviewCards.back: Because people drift toward the choice that takes the least work, so a habit with fewer steps in front of it happens more often.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the small chores that stand before a habit and clearing them away so starting takes almost nothing.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to my habit and have to fetch something first, I store that thing where I sit, so it is already there next time.
When I catch myself thinking I just need more willpower, I write down each step before that habit starts and get one ready ahead today.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before bed tonight, set out everything one skipped habit needs at the exact spot where you'll do it, so starting takes one move.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, pick the habit you skipped most, list the steps it takes to start, and remove or get ready ahead one more of them.

chapters.title: Start Every New Habit With a Two-Minute Version
chapters.hook: A brand-new punching bag, and a 45-minute plan taped beside it. By Wednesday, that plan will be the reason the bag hangs untouched.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to start a new habit big, with a full workout or an hour of study, so it counts. But the first version should take under two minutes, because a habit has to take root before it can grow.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you start a new habit, shrink it to a version that takes under two minutes.
chapters.tryThisNow: Pick one habit you've been meaning to start and do a version of it that takes under two minutes, right now.

memorableLines.text: Make the first step too small to skip, and the rest follows.

breakdown.fastRead:
A new punching bag hangs from a beam in Omar's basement. Taped beside it is his plan: a 45-minute boxing workout every morning at six, starting Monday. Anything shorter feels like cheating. But a start that big runs on first-day excitement. By Wednesday he'll be tired, and one skipped morning will turn into a month.

James Clear's answer is the Two-Minute Rule: when you start a new habit, cut it down until it takes less than two minutes. Read one page instead of a book. That easy first step is a gateway habit, a door into the rest. The dancer Twyla Tharp starts each morning by stepping outside and waving down a taxi to take her to the gym. That taxi is her start, and her whole workout follows. A habit has to be in place before it can be improved, so first get good at showing up, then make it bigger.

So Omar rewrites the plan. The habit now is to walk downstairs, pull on his gloves and hit the bag twenty times. On slow mornings he stops there and still counts the day. Most mornings, with the gloves already on, he keeps going. When you start a new habit, cut it to a version under two minutes, and you'll keep showing up until it can grow.

examples.title: Tools piling up on the workbench
examples.scenario: Daisuke runs a small carpentry shop, and by evening his bench is buried in saws, clamps and chisels. He has decided that from tonight, he will spend thirty minutes after closing cleaning every tool and hanging it on the pegboard. It's six o'clock, his back aches, and the radio is still playing. He looks at the pile and reaches for his jacket.
examples.whatToDo: Hang the one saw you used most today back on the pegboard, and call tonight's habit done.
examples.whyItMatters: A start that small still happens on a tired evening, and once he is at the pegboard, putting back the rest is easy.

examples.title: Three Sundays of skipped budgeting
examples.scenario: Sadia wanted to stop running short before payday, so she set aside every Sunday evening for two hours with her bank statements and a budget spreadsheet. The first Sunday went well. Then she skipped one, then two more. Now three weeks of spending sit unchecked, and just opening the laptop makes her stomach drop.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the two-hour Sunday session and leave the missed weeks for now. Tonight, type in just today's spending, which takes under two minutes.
examples.whyItMatters: The big session is what she kept putting off. A two-minute entry gets her showing up again, and the habit can grow from there.

examples.title: When the teacher says two minutes is nothing
examples.scenario: Chloe is two weeks into singing lessons, and her teacher wants thirty minutes of scales every day. After a week of skipped practice, Chloe suggests starting with two minutes instead. Her teacher frowns over the piano. "Two minutes won't train your voice. If you're serious, do the half hour." Chloe pays for the lessons herself, and she hates the thought of wasting them.
examples.whatToDo: Offer the teacher a plan: two minutes of scales daily this week, then a few more minutes each week until you reach thirty.
examples.whyItMatters: A habit has to be in place before it can grow, so the teacher gets the full half hour later instead of none.

questions.prompt: You want to start doing push-ups each morning. A fitness app offers a 20-minute beginner plan, and tomorrow is your first day. What do you do?
choices: Get down and do five push-ups, then stop for the day.
Do the app's full 20-minute plan, but only three days a week.
Do ten minutes of the plan, adding one minute each day.
questions.explanation: It's your first day, so the habit needs a start under two minutes. Five push-ups get done even on a tired morning. Ten minutes, or the full plan three days a week, is still a big start.

questions.prompt: A nurse decides to study for a promotion exam. She puts a full hour in her calendar for every evening, starting that night. By week two she has stopped. Which of her three reasons was the trap?
choices: "Evenings fit best around my shifts at the hospital."
"Putting each session in my phone calendar will help me remember it."
"Only a full hour from day one will count as progress."
questions.explanation: Fitting study around her shifts and writing it in her calendar are sound. The trap was believing only a full hour from the first night counts. That big start is what she stopped showing up for.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you, "From Monday, I'm doing a full hour of yoga every morning before work." What is your best reply?
choices: "Begin by rolling out your mat and doing one pose a day."
"Add a weekend class as well, so the yoga sticks a lot faster."
"Keep the full hour, but begin once your week is quieter."
questions.explanation: Your friend is starting a new habit on Monday, so the first version should take under two minutes. Rolling out the mat for one pose leads into more. A quieter week still leaves a full hour waiting.

questions.prompt: An office worker wanted to learn to type without looking at the keys. She began with one typing drill a day, under two minutes. Six weeks later she practices for twenty minutes most days. Why did starting so small work?
choices: Short daily drills teach as much as long sessions over time.
The quick drills got her excited enough to push on into longer sessions.
It became a daily routine first, and only then did it grow.
questions.explanation: She did one tiny drill every day before ever practicing longer. A habit has to be in place before it can be improved. Excitement fades, so it can't explain six weeks of steady practice.

questions.prompt: You want to start cycling to work, a forty-minute ride. There's no way to make the ride itself take under two minutes. What's the best way to begin?
choices: Wait to start until the longer summer days make the ride easier.
Each morning, put on your helmet and wheel the bike outside.
Ride in only on Fridays until the trip feels normal.
questions.explanation: The ride can't shrink, but its start can. Putting on your helmet and wheeling the bike out takes under two minutes and leads into the ride. Fridays only still means the whole ride.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I've cut my plan to practice calligraphy, the art of fancy handwriting, from an hour a night to twenty minutes. That's small enough now." What do you say back?
choices: "Good, and stop right at twenty minutes, even on nights you want more."
"Twenty minutes is still a lot, so begin by writing one letter."
"Good, now plan how you'll build back up to the hour."
questions.explanation: Cutting the hour was a good step, but twenty minutes still asks for a real push each night. The missing piece is a start under two minutes, like one letter. Building back up comes after the habit is in place.

questions.prompt: A man wanted to start writing a blog but kept skipping it. To fix that, he made himself sit down for a full hour every evening, phone off. After two weeks he gave up. Why did forcing it fail?
choices: Every evening began with a full hour he had to force himself into.
He had no clear target, like one finished post every single week.
The hour was just too long, and forty minutes each night would have lasted.
questions.explanation: He kept skipping because the start was too big, and his fix kept the full hour. Forty minutes is still a big start. A version under two minutes is easy to show up for.

reviewCards.front: A man set aside three hours every Saturday to learn watercolor painting and gave up after the second weekend. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He began with a version too big to keep showing up for. Wetting a brush and painting one stroke would have built the habit first.

reviewCards.front: In your own words: how small should the first version of a new habit be, and why?
reviewCards.back: Small enough to do in under two minutes, because you have to get good at showing up before the habit can be made bigger.

reviewCards.front: You want to start clearing your email inbox every morning, but it holds thousands of messages.
reviewCards.back: Start with a version under two minutes, like opening the inbox and dealing with the top three messages. Grow it once you show up daily.

reviewCards.front: Why does a big first session, like an hour of exercise, so often end a new habit within the first week?
reviewCards.back: It runs on first-day excitement, and once that fades, the big start is easy to put off. A two-minute start still gets done on tired days.

reviewCards.front: Before a habit can be improved, it first has to ...
reviewCards.back: ... be in place, so start with a version you can do in under two minutes and make it bigger once you keep showing up.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Making the opening move of any new routine small enough to do even on a tired day.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I set my alarm the night before starting a new habit, I choose one act, under two minutes, to do first thing after waking.
When I catch myself putting off a new habit because it feels too big, I cut it to a version under two minutes and do that right away.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, pick a habit you once started big and then dropped. Do a version of it that takes under two minutes, and stop there.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each day this week, do the same two-minute start at the same moment. If you haven't missed a day by the weekend, add a minute or two for next week.

chapters.title: Decide Now So Your Tired Self Can't Back Out
chapters.hook: The person who plans your Monday yoga class is not the one who decides whether you go. That is the sleepy you at seven.
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that sticking to a habit takes willpower in the moment. The trouble is that the moment finds you tired and tempted, so make the choice earlier, while you still want the habit.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you feel strong, make one choice today that locks your future self into the good habit.
chapters.tryThisNow: Move your phone charger out of your bedroom and into a kitchen drawer before you sit down this evening.

memorableLines.text: Decide on your good day so your bad day has nothing left to decide.

breakdown.fastRead:
Tonight at midnight, with your alarm set for six, you'll probably still be scrolling on your phone. How do you make that tired you stop, when you already know you won't want to? James Clear's answer is a commitment device, a choice you make now that controls what you can do later. You make it while you think clearly, and it holds when you don't.

The writer Victor Hugo needed one. He had promised his publisher a new book and kept putting it off, until the publisher set a firm deadline. So Hugo had his assistant lock all his clothes in a big chest. He kept only a large shawl, so he had nothing to wear outside. He stayed home, wrote, and finished The Hunchback of Notre Dame early.

The usual answer is more willpower. But midnight finds you tired, the easy option in your hand, and the fight returns every night. Hugo took the fight away. Clear would have you add locks until the good habit is the only path left, and you can start with one today. Tonight, that could mean moving your phone charger to a kitchen drawer, so the phone sleeps there. Make one choice while you feel strong, one that leaves your later self only the good option, and the hard moment will need no willpower.

examples.title: A flat that only gets cleaned for guests
examples.scenario: Elena's flat only gets a proper clean when someone is coming over. Most weeks the floors stay sticky and the windows grow grey, and she hates walking in after work. It is Sunday afternoon, she slept well, and she feels ready to fix it. Her phone lights up with a message from an old friend asking when they can finally catch up.
examples.whatToDo: Reply now and invite the friend to dinner at your flat this Friday and every second Friday after, so the cleaning has a fixed deadline.
examples.whyItMatters: She settles it on a rested Sunday. On a tired Thursday the guest is already coming, so the cleaning doesn't wait on her willpower.

examples.title: Homework fights after a long workday
examples.scenario: Every school night Adaeze promises herself she'll be firm: maths worksheet first, then her son's cartoons. By six she is worn out from work, and he starts bargaining for ten more minutes. Last night it ended with both of them shouting and the worksheet still blank. Now it is Saturday morning, the house is quiet, and she already dreads Monday.
examples.whatToDo: Tell your son sorry for last night's shouting, then set the home Wi-Fi to switch off his devices from six to seven on school nights.
examples.whyItMatters: Set on a calm Saturday, the rule holds at six on Monday, so a tired parent has no fight left to lose.

examples.title: Patient notes that follow her home
examples.scenario: Irina, a nurse at a busy walk-in clinic, kept typing patient notes at home until midnight. On a fresh Monday she decided her work laptop would stay locked in her clinic office each night. It worked for two evenings. On the third, she opened the notes system on her own phone, typed until one, and dragged herself through her eight o'clock patients.
examples.whatToDo: Before leaving the clinic on Tuesday, sign out of the notes system on your own phone and delete it, so the office laptop is the only way in.
examples.whyItMatters: A lock with a gap is no lock. While one way in stays open, her tired midnight self will take it.

questions.prompt: Bjorn wants to be asleep by eleven. On a sharp, rested Sunday he decides the laptop will close at ten thirty each night, and he leaves it plugged in on his bedside table. By Wednesday he has been up past one every night. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: "Sunday is a good day to decide this, since I feel sharp."
"When it's late, I'll simply find the strength to close it."
"Sleeping by eleven will make my mornings at work easier."
questions.explanation: Deciding on a sharp Sunday was smart, and the sleep goal was sound. The trap was trusting late-night Bjorn. With the laptop plugged in by his bed, every night became a fresh fight he lost.

questions.prompt: A friend has been skipping their Saturday morning drawing class. Work has been hectic, but today, Thursday, they feel full of energy. They say, "This Saturday I'll just force myself out of bed." What's your best reply?
choices: "Arrange today for a classmate to collect you on Saturday morning."
"Wait until work calms down, then start the class fresh."
"Sign up for a second weekly class, so drawing feels more serious."
questions.explanation: They feel strong today, so today is the moment to settle Saturday. With a classmate arriving, the choice is already made. A second class only adds another morning for the sleepy Saturday self to skip.

questions.prompt: Cyrus kept spending his pay before the month was out. On payday, feeling organised, he set up a transfer that moves part of his pay into savings the same morning it arrives. Months later his savings keep growing. Why has this worked?
choices: Watching the savings grow each month keeps him keen to save.
The money moves before he ever gets the chance to spend it.
Having less spare cash lying around slowly teaches him to want fewer things.
questions.explanation: The transfer runs the morning his pay arrives. He made the choice once, on an organised day, and nothing is left for later to decide. Watching savings grow doesn't explain why the spending stopped first.

questions.prompt: Most nights you eat spoonfuls from the big tub of ice cream you buy for your kids. You had planned to stop buying it, but you've promised the kids ice cream after Sunday dinner, and they'll hold you to it. You're in the shop now. What do you do?
choices: Buy the big tub as usual and promise yourself you'll leave it alone.
Buy one small tub per child, with nothing extra in the freezer.
Leave ice cream off the list and serve the kids fruit.
questions.explanation: In the shop, you're thinking clearly. One small tub per child keeps your promise to the kids and leaves nothing for late-night spoonfuls. Serving fruit breaks that promise, and a big tub plus a promise to yourself hands the choice back to your tired evening self.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I'm fired up tonight, so I've decided to go to the 7 a.m. boxing class twice a week. It's in my calendar now, so that's settled." What do you say back?
choices: "Buy your own boxing gloves tonight, while you're keen, so it feels real."
"Each night before class, decide again whether you'll go at seven."
"Book and pay for the next four classes tonight, while you're keen."
questions.explanation: A calendar entry only reminds, and at 7 a.m. the friend can still roll over. Booking and paying tonight settles those mornings in advance. New gloves feel like a step but leave each early morning just as open.

questions.prompt: Ajay wanted to stop answering work messages at the family dinner table. Each evening he kept his work phone in his pocket and told himself to stay strong. Within a week he was replying at most dinners, and his kids had stopped talking to him at the table. Why did his plan fall apart?
choices: He left the deciding until dinnertime, when messages were already coming in.
He didn't care enough about family dinners to keep his promise.
He tried every dinner at once instead of starting with one a week.
questions.explanation: The phone sat in his pocket, so every dinner became a new fight at a tired hour, with messages arriving. He did care. What he never did was settle the matter before dinner, on a clear day.

questions.prompt: You keep meaning to help at the animal shelter on Sunday mornings, but by Sunday the sofa always wins. The shelter runs a Sunday rota with an online sign-up sheet. It's Tuesday lunchtime and you feel keen. What's the move?
choices: Try one Sunday first and join the rota if it suits.
Lay out your old jeans and boots on Saturday night, ready to go.
Put your name on every Sunday slot of this month's shelter rota.
questions.explanation: Tuesday is when you feel keen, so that's when to settle Sunday. With your name on the rota, people expect you. Trying one Sunday first leaves that Sunday to the sofa, which keeps winning.

reviewCards.back: Delete the listings app and sign out of the site now, so the 1 a.m. you has nothing to open.

reviewCards.front: Why does a choice made on a good day still work on a bad one?
reviewCards.back: You make it while you think clearly, and once made it controls what you can do, so your tired self never gets a vote.

reviewCards.front: Instead of counting on willpower when the urge arrives, you ...
reviewCards.back: ... make a choice earlier, while you feel strong, that puts the bad option out of reach before the urge ever comes.

reviewCards.front: On a clear-headed Monday, Oona swore off online poker at night. She left her card saved on the poker site and planned to just say no. By Friday she had played three nights. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She decided at a good moment but made nothing binding. The saved card left the real choice to late-night Oona. Deleting it on Monday would have closed that door.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Using your clear-headed hours to settle, ahead of time, what your tired self will be able to do.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking I'll be strong enough later, I make one change on the spot that takes the easy option away, like moving my phone charger out of the bedroom.
When I get home after a good day with energy to spare, I use that energy to make one choice that settles my weakest hour of the evening in advance.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, pick the habit you most often drop when tired. While you feel fresh, make one change that settles it ahead of time, such as deleting an app or signing up somewhere people expect you.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each Sunday, while rested, name the habit most likely to slip this week and make one choice that settles it in advance. On Saturday, check whether it held, and close any gap you find.

chapters.title: Give Slow Habits a Quick Payoff
chapters.hook: Germs are too small to see, and a healthy child looks the same each day. So what got families in Karachi washing their hands?
chapters.counterintuition: You know the habit is good for you, so the later benefit should keep you going. It sounds right, and it fails for one reason: your brain cares most about what you feel right now. Give the habit a small reward the moment you finish.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a good habit only pays off later, give yourself a small reward the moment you finish.
chapters.tryThisNow: Call a friend you enjoy talking to the moment you finish one good habit today, and make that chat your treat.

memorableLines.text: Good habits pay later, so pay yourself the second you finish.

breakdown.fastRead:
Good reasons make weak fuel for a habit. What keeps it going is how it feels as you finish. James Clear shows this with Stephen Luby, a public health worker in Karachi, Pakistan. He gave families a fancy soap that foamed well and smelled nice. Washing hands felt good every time, so it became a habit, and diarrhea in children fell by 52 percent. The healthy children came later, but the pleasure came at the sink.

On paper, a healthy future should beat a moment of effort. Clear explains why it rarely does. The human brain grew up in a world where actions paid off or hurt right away. Today most good habits pay off later, while bad habits feel good now. Clear sums it up as the Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change. What feels good right away gets repeated, and what feels bad right away gets avoided.

So give a slow habit a quick payoff. Pick a good habit you keep skipping and a small treat for the second you finish. To spend less, open a savings account and move the money from each skipped purchase into it. The treat gets the habit going until it feels like part of who you are. Once a good habit pays you the moment it ends, you stop skipping it.

breakdown.fullRead:
Good reasons make weak fuel for a habit. What keeps it going is how it feels as you finish. That sounds backwards, because most of us believe that once we see the benefit, we will act on it. James Clear argues the other way, and he starts with soap.

Stephen Luby was a public health worker in Karachi, Pakistan. He wanted families there to wash their hands with soap. So he gave them a fancy soap that foamed well and smelled nice. Washing hands stopped being a chore and became a small pleasure. People kept doing it until it was a habit. Diarrhea in children fell by 52 percent.

Look at why it worked. The real payoff of clean hands is out of sight. Germs are too small to see, and a child who stays well looks the same from one day to the next. The lather and the smell, though, came at the sink every single time. People felt good the moment they rinsed, so they came back. The health benefit rode along on that small pleasure.

Clear explains why we need that pleasure. The human brain grew up in what he calls an immediate-return world, where what you did paid off or hurt you right away. You ate, and your hunger went. You ran from danger, and you were safe. Today we live in a delayed-return world, where most payoffs come later. You work now and get paid weeks later. You save now and use the money years from now.

That gap turns habits upside down. Most good habits cost you something now and pay you later. Most bad habits pay you now and cost you later. A late-night snack tastes good tonight, and its cost shows up months down the line. Clear sums this up as the Cardinal Rule of Behavior Change. What feels good right away gets repeated. What feels bad right away gets avoided.

This is why the later payoff seems like it should be enough. You make plans with the future in mind, and on paper a healthy future easily beats a moment of effort. But you act in the moment, not in the plan. In the moment, your brain counts what it feels. A benefit you can only picture keeps losing to a pleasure you can taste.

So give a slow habit a quick payoff. First, pick a good habit you keep skipping. Next, choose a small treat you enjoy and can have the second you finish, every time. Some good habits mean not doing something, and skipping a thing leaves you nothing to see. To spend less, open a savings account. Each time you skip a purchase, move that money into it at once, and watch the number grow.

The treat does not have to carry the habit forever. It gets the habit going while the real payoff is still far away. Over time, the habit starts to feel like part of who you are, and that keeps it alive. Once a good habit pays you the moment it ends, you stop skipping it.

examples.title: Pitch emails with no reply in sight
examples.scenario: Kojo is a freelance photographer who works from a desk in the corner of his flat. Every morning he is meant to send three pitch emails to new clients. Replies take weeks, and most never come, so lately he skips the emails and edits photos instead. Today he has just sent the third one. A new camera magazine sits unopened beside a stack of photos to edit.
examples.whatToDo: Pick up the magazine now and read it for ten minutes, as the payoff for the three emails just sent.
examples.whyItMatters: Clients may answer in weeks, or never. The magazine pays him today, and what feels good right away is what gets repeated.

examples.title: A job ad that made studying feel worse
examples.scenario: Wanjiru takes an online project management course in the evenings, hoping for a promotion next year. To stay on track, she made a photo of the job ad her phone background and reminded herself of the raise every night. She is now three lessons behind. Each time she opens the course page, she feels a stab of guilt and closes it again.
examples.whatToDo: Take the job ad off your phone background. Tonight, do just one lesson, then make your favourite tea the minute it's done.
examples.whyItMatters: The job ad made every study night feel bad, and what feels bad gets avoided. A treat after each lesson pulls her back.

examples.title: Ten minutes between haircuts
examples.scenario: Emine cuts hair in a busy salon and gets about ten minutes between clients to eat. She and her partner, Goran, are saving for a deposit on a flat, so she brings lunch from home. The flat feels years away. By Thursday her lunch box sits untouched, and she buys noodles next door. "I don't have time for little treats," she tells Goran.
examples.whatToDo: Open a shared savings account with Goran tonight. On each day you eat the packed lunch, move the noodle money into it from your phone.
examples.whyItMatters: Moving the money takes seconds and the balance grows at once, so skipping the noodles pays her today, not years from now.

questions.prompt: A friend has started walking the forty minutes to work to get fit by spring. She says picturing herself in spring will keep her going. What do you tell her?
choices: "Read up on what walking does for your heart, so the goal feels more real."
"Plan a big lunch out each weekend if you walked every single day."
"Buy yourself a hot chocolate as soon as you reach the office each day."
questions.explanation: Spring is months away, so picturing it gives her nothing on the walk itself. A hot chocolate on arrival pays her the moment each walk ends. A weekend lunch comes days after most walks.

questions.prompt: Every time a woman leaves a shirt she wanted on the rack, she moves its price into a savings account named after a trip next summer. She sees the new balance a second later. Months on, she still does it. Why did this work?
choices: Seeing the trip fund grow was a pleasure then, long before the trip.
Leaving each shirt behind stung, and she worked hard to avoid that sting again.
Naming the account after the trip kept that faraway goal in view.
questions.explanation: The trip was months off, but the balance grew a second after each skipped shirt. That quick pleasure is what got repeated. A sting would make her avoid the habit, not keep it.

questions.prompt: You've started a nightly ten-minute tidy of your work desk at home, with a square of good chocolate as your treat. Tonight the chocolate is gone, and the shop is shut until morning. What do you do?
choices: Skip the tidy tonight, and do a longer one when the chocolate is back.
Do the tidy now, and have two squares tomorrow to make up.
Finish the tidy, then swap in a different treat you can have tonight.
questions.explanation: The shop is shut until morning, so chocolate can't follow tonight's tidy. Another treat tonight keeps the quick payoff. Two squares tomorrow arrive a day late, too far from the tidy.

questions.prompt: A friend has started a short yoga video each morning. "I bought a lovely new mat as my treat for starting," he says, "so the reward part is done." What do you say?
choices: "Buy a fancy strap as a second gift, so starting feels even more special."
"The mat came just once, so have a treat after every session too."
"Pin a list of yoga's health gains right beside the mat."
questions.explanation: The mat was one treat at the start, so each session still pays him nothing. A small treat after every session makes each one feel good. A list of health gains changes nothing in the moment.

questions.prompt: Every Sunday, a man means to spend fifteen minutes writing his budget, to clear his card debt by next year. Each time, he tells himself how good debt-free will feel. By the fourth Sunday he has stopped. Why did his plan fail?
choices: Clearing the card was a year off, and the budget gave him nothing then.
Budgets are dull by nature, and no trick makes sorting numbers feel fun.
He set too big a goal, since clearing the card in a year felt huge.
questions.explanation: His only payoff, a clear card, was a year away, and each Sunday's budget felt like nothing in the moment. A budget can be dull, which is exactly why it needed a quick treat.

questions.prompt: You put on sunscreen each morning to protect your skin for years ahead. The bottle sits by your toothbrush and you see it daily, but putting it on feels sticky and dull. You skip it most days. What change do you make?
choices: Drop a coin in a jar as a fine on each morning you skip it.
Switch to a kind with a smell you love, so the routine feels nice.
Play a song you love first, so you're in the mood for it.
questions.explanation: You already see the bottle daily, so the trouble is how it feels. A smell you love makes each morning's sunscreen pleasant on the spot. A fine makes the habit feel worse, so you'd avoid it more.

questions.prompt: A woman began walking her dog twenty minutes longer each evening, to be fitter by summer. Summer was five months off, and she quit within a month. Which of her three reasons was the trap?
choices: The fitness to come would be reason enough to keep it up.
Going right after dinner each night meant she would not forget to go.
Twenty extra minutes was small enough to fit into any evening.
questions.explanation: Her payoff was five months off, so each walk gave her nothing that evening. Walking after dinner and keeping it to twenty minutes were sound. Counting on future fitness to carry her was the trap.

reviewCards.front: You've begun backing up your laptop every Friday, a habit that only pays off if the laptop ever dies. Most Fridays you skip it. What do you do?
reviewCards.back: Pick a small treat you enjoy, like an episode of a favourite show, and have it the moment the backup finishes, so each Friday's backup pays you then.

reviewCards.front: When a good habit means not buying something, the way to make each skip pay off at once is to ...
reviewCards.back: ... move the money you didn't spend into a savings account straight away, so every skip shows up as a bigger number.

reviewCards.front: Someone began clearing their work inbox every Friday afternoon, with a big dinner out promised for each month they kept it up. By week three they had stopped. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: The dinner sat weeks after each Friday, so clearing the inbox gave them nothing in the moment. A small treat straight after each session would have kept it going.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Pairing each good habit that pays off slowly with a quick, pleasant payoff that lands the second it's done.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself skipping a good habit whose payoff feels far off, I pick one small treat for right after it and do the habit now.
When I unpack my weekly food shop at home, I move the price of any snack I left on the shelf into my savings account.

chapters.title: One Missed Day Is Fine. Two Start a New Habit.
chapters.hook: The card taped to your mirror shows twenty ticks in a row, then one empty square. Starting a clean card on Monday feels sensible.
chapters.counterintuition: The usual advice is that a broken streak calls for a fresh start next week. Coming back at the very next chance works better, because one miss does little harm, while a second miss starts a new habit of skipping.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you skip a habit once, do it the very next time, even if only a small version.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write down the number of minutes you will do on the day after a miss, and tape it today where you do your habit.

memorableLines.text: Miss once if you must, then show up the very next time.

Even a short, weak session on a bad day counts, because it keeps you the kind of person who does the habit.

examples.title: The morning after a stomach bug
examples.scenario: Every morning for a month, Lakshmi has done fifteen swings with her kettlebell, an iron weight with a handle, by her bedroom window. Yesterday a stomach bug kept her in bed all day. This morning she feels weak, and the weight looks heavier than before. She thinks she might as well rest and restart properly next week. She stands at the window, deciding.
examples.whatToDo: Do five slow swings this morning, however weak they feel, and count the day as done, so yesterday stays a single miss.
examples.whyItMatters: One sick day does little harm. Waiting a week would start a pattern of skipping, and even weak swings keep her someone who trains.

examples.title: Three skipped van checks
examples.scenario: Thabo, a plumber, started checking the parts in his van each morning before his first call. Last Tuesday he overslept and skipped it, so he decided to start clean the following Monday. By Thursday he had skipped two more checks. That afternoon, at a leaking kitchen sink, he found no spare valve on board and lost two hours driving to the supplier.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the Monday plan. Before the next call, check the parts for the jobs left today, then do the full check each morning again.
examples.whyItMatters: Each skip since Tuesday has made skipping his routine. Checking even a few parts at the next chance stops the slide before it costs more.

examples.title: A low mark on a practice night
examples.scenario: Shreya, a first-year chemistry student, does ten practice problems at her dorm desk every evening. Last night she skipped them for a friend's birthday. This afternoon her lab quiz came back with a low mark circled in red, and she feels stupid. Opening the problem book tonight feels like reading that mark again. She tells her roommate she will start fresh once she feels like herself.
examples.whatToDo: Do two easy problems now, before the feeling grows through the evening, and let that shaky start count as tonight's session.
examples.whyItMatters: Last night was one miss. A shaky session on a bad day stops a second and keeps her someone who does the work.

questions.prompt: Minh holds a plank every night, keeping his body stiff and straight on his forearms, and ticks a chart afterward. He missed Tuesday after a long shift. On Wednesday, still tired, he held it for twenty seconds instead of a minute. Three months on, he still planks nightly. Why did that short Wednesday plank matter more than his full planks on other nights?
choices: It kept one skipped night from becoming a pattern.
It made up for part of the minute he lost on Tuesday.
It put one more tick on his nightly chart.
questions.explanation: Every night adds a tick, and twenty seconds could not replace Tuesday's minute. Wednesday mattered because it came straight after a miss, so skipping never got the chance to become his habit.

questions.prompt: Leticia does twenty minutes of tai chi, a slow, flowing exercise, in her back yard each morning. She missed Monday's session. On Tuesday it is pouring, and she has five minutes before she leaves for her train. What should she do before leaving?
choices: Do a double session in the yard on Wednesday instead.
Do five minutes of the moves in the kitchen before leaving.
Wait for a dry morning and do the full twenty minutes then.
questions.explanation: Monday is already missed, so Tuesday is the morning that counts. Five minutes indoors keeps it to one miss. A double session on Wednesday, or waiting for a dry day, means a second skip in a row.

questions.prompt: Your friend Yosef practices card tricks for half an hour every night. He says, "I skipped last night, but I'm not quitting. I'll do my full half hour tonight if I'm home before nine." His shift often runs late. What is your best reply?
choices: "Good plan. Don't feel bad about last night; one miss is fine."
"Good plan. If you're late, do one trick for five minutes."
"Good plan. Ask your flatmate to check that you practiced."
questions.explanation: He plans to come back tonight, but his shift often runs late, so the full half hour may not happen. Five minutes of one trick still counts. Kind words or a flatmate's check leave that gap open.

questions.prompt: Tove practiced her puzzle cube for fifteen minutes each night. She missed one night, so she decided to start again on the first of the month, nine days away. When the first came, she never picked the cube up. Why did the fresh start fail?
choices: She needed a stronger reason to want to practice.
One missed night showed the habit had never really been solid.
By then, skipping every night had become her new routine.
questions.explanation: She waited more than a week for the first, so night after night went by without the cube. By then skipping was the habit. The one missed night had done little harm on its own.

questions.prompt: Paola does five minutes of balance exercises each morning to strengthen her ankle, and ticks a chart on her bedroom door. She spent last night at her sister's and missed yesterday's set. This morning she is home, with her usual five minutes free. What does she do now?
choices: Do her balance set this morning at the usual time.
Move the chart to where she will see it each morning.
Let this week go and start fresh on Monday.
questions.explanation: Yesterday is already one miss, and she has her usual five minutes this morning. Doing the set now keeps it to one. Moving the chart or waiting for Monday lets a second morning slip by.

questions.prompt: Kenta gave his new puppy a ten-minute training session every evening. He missed Tuesday, then skipped the rest of the week. He told himself three things along the way. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: "The run of evenings is broken, so I'll restart next week."
"One evening off won't undo what the puppy has learned."
"A short session on Wednesday would still be fine if I'm tired."
questions.explanation: One missed evening does little harm, and a short session on a tired night still counts. Treating Tuesday as a broken run, and waiting for next week, turned one miss into a whole week off.

questions.prompt: On Wednesday evening a friend tells you, "I've sent one job application every weekday for three weeks. Today I didn't, so this week is ruined. I'll start properly on Monday." What do you tell them?
choices: "Fair enough, a clean start on Monday will keep you keen."
"Spend a few days working out why today slipped."
"Send a short one tomorrow and drop the Monday plan."
questions.explanation: It is Wednesday, so waiting for Monday means two more weekdays without applying. One short application tomorrow keeps today a single miss. Spending days on why it slipped lets those same days pass.

reviewCards.back: One slip happens to everyone and does little harm. The second miss is where a new pattern of skipping begins, so coming back at once stops the slide.

reviewCards.front: When you miss a habit once, the best time to start again is ...
reviewCards.back: ... the very next time it comes round, even with a short, shaky version, not a fresh start next week.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do the day after you skip a habit?
reviewCards.back: Do it again at the next chance, even in a small way. One miss is normal, but two in a row start a new pattern.

reviewCards.front: You practice a short work speech aloud each evening. You skipped last night, and tonight friends are coming over until late.
reviewCards.back: Run through just the opening once before they arrive. A short run tonight keeps last night a single miss.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Getting straight back to a habit after a slip, at whatever size the day allows.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I get home the day after I skipped a habit, I do a small version of it before I sit down to eat.
When I catch myself thinking I'll just start fresh on Monday, I do a few minutes of the habit today and tick it off.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one habit you have let slide in the last few weeks. Before you go to bed tonight, do a small piece of it and mark it done.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each day this week, check which habits you skipped. For each one, do a short version at the very next chance, before a second day goes by.

chapters.title: Put a Price on Breaking Your Own Promises
chapters.hook: Promise yourself, and it breaks quietly with no one watching. Promise your sister, with twenty dollars riding on every slip, and it holds.
chapters.counterintuition: We tend to think that if we really want to change, we should manage it alone. What works is a written deal with a penalty that someone else signs, since we care what others think, and the cost lands right away.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When you keep breaking a promise to yourself, write a penalty into a contract someone else signs.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write one promise you keep breaking and a cost for each slip, then send it to a friend tonight and ask them to sign.

memorableLines.text: Put a price on each slip, and let a friend collect it.

breakdown.fastRead:
Why would a man who wants to lose weight agree to pay $200 every day he skips writing down his meals? It sounds like punishing himself for his own goal. James Clear calls it smart.

A broken promise costs nothing on the day, so Clear gives it a price. His tool is a habit contract, a written deal that says what you will do and what you pay if you don't. One or two people sign it and hold you to it. That man was Bryan Harris, a business owner in Nashville. He signed one with his wife and his personal trainer, promising to write down every meal and weigh himself. Every day without food notes cost him $200, paid to his trainer. Breaking the deal also meant dressing up for work and on Sunday mornings for the rest of that three-month stretch. Later he raised the stakes with more cash fines, and the weight came off.

Most of us just try harder alone. But a promise nobody else sees is easy to bend at nine at night. Clear calls the person who watches an accountability partner, and we care what that person thinks of us. People keep a hard promise once breaking it carries a written penalty that someone they care about has signed on to collect.

examples.title: Mondays at the record shop
examples.scenario: Kenji runs a one-person online shop selling secondhand vinyl records. Every Monday he promises himself he'll photograph and list twenty new ones. For six Mondays the crates have sat unopened by his desk, and sales have dropped because the shop looks stale. Tonight he opens his planner to write the same promise again, pen over the page.
examples.whatToDo: Write the deal instead: twenty records listed by Monday night, or $30 to his friend Esra that evening. Ask Esra to sign and check the shop Tuesday.
examples.whyItMatters: A skipped Monday now costs him money the same night, and a friend whose opinion he cares about will see it.

examples.title: Six weeks before the audition
examples.scenario: Daniel wants to audition for a friend's covers band in March. In January he swore to himself he'd practise twenty minutes on his drum kit every night. Whenever he skipped, he told himself he'd catch up at the weekend. He rarely did. Six weeks in, he still can't play the audition song through.
examples.whatToDo: Own up to his friend about the skipped nights. Then write a deal, $10 paid to that friend each missed night, and have them sign it.
examples.whyItMatters: A promise only he could see was easy to bend. With his friend signed on, each missed night costs him $10 that same night.

examples.title: A friend who won't take the money
examples.scenario: Yetunde, sixteen, keeps promising herself an hour of chemistry revision after school, and keeps skipping it. Her mock exams start in three weeks. At lunch she slides a deal across the canteen table: each skipped afternoon, she buys her best friend Dalia lunch. Dalia pushes it back. "I'm not taking your money. Just do it, you're clever."
examples.whatToDo: Thank Dalia, then take the deal to someone who will collect, like her older cousin, and have the cousin sign it today.
examples.whyItMatters: A signer who won't collect leaves skipping free again. The deal only works when someone holds her to it.

questions.prompt: Your brother signed your deal: $10 to him for each night you leave the kitchen a mess. Three times now he has waved it off and said keep it. What do you do now?
choices: Raise the fine to $30, so your brother can't wave it away.
Ask a friend who'd gladly accept the $10 to stand in for him.
Keep the deal, and put the $10 in a savings tin yourself each time.
questions.explanation: Your brother has waved off the fine three times, so no one is holding you to the deal. A friend who will take the money makes each messy night cost you. A bigger fine he waves off still costs nothing.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I've skipped piano practice most of this month. So I wrote down twenty minutes a day, and my sister signed it. Sorted." What is your best reply?
choices: "Show it to your piano teacher too, so two people are watching you."
"See how this week goes, and add a cost if needed."
"Add what each skipped day costs you, and who it goes to."
questions.explanation: The note says what your friend will do and has a signer, but a skipped day still costs nothing. Naming the price and who gets it fills that gap. After a month of skipping, waiting a week just adds free skips.

questions.prompt: A man promises himself he'll bring lunch from home instead of buying it. Whenever he slips, he tells himself he'll make up for it next week. Two months on, he's still buying lunch most days. Why did his plan fall apart?
choices: Each slip was free that day, and no one else saw it.
He just didn't want the change badly enough to stick with it for long.
He needed a bigger reason, like saving for a summer trip.
questions.explanation: His only answer to a slip was a private plan to make up for it next week. So each slip cost nothing on the day, and nobody saw it. Wanting it more would not have changed that.

questions.prompt: Most evenings this month you've skipped your after-dinner walk, telling yourself you'll go tomorrow. Your partner offers to help. What do you set up tonight?
choices: Agree with your partner that you pay $5 the night you skip.
Agree with your partner that they'll ask you each night.
Agree with your partner that you pay $20 after a week of skipping.
questions.explanation: You keep pushing each walk to tomorrow. Paying $5 on the night you skip makes the slip cost you at once. A weekly $20 lets each night slide, and a question alone costs you nothing.

questions.prompt: A man has skipped most evenings of study this month for his citizenship test, two months away. He decides to keep going without telling anyone. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: "I've already lost a whole month, so I truly can't afford to lose more."
"If I really want to pass, I can do this on my own."
"Passing this test matters a great deal to me and my family."
questions.explanation: Losing a month and caring about the test are both true. The trap is trusting that wanting it will carry him alone, when a month of skipped evenings has cost him nothing on the day.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I've broken my no-gaming-after-midnight rule for weeks. This time I'll just be tough on myself. I'd hate to drag my flatmate into it." What do you tell her?
choices: "Ask your flatmate to claim one chore from you for each late night."
"Give $10 to charity for each late night, and keep count yourself."
"Buy yourself a new game at the month's end if you keep to it."
questions.explanation: Weeks of being tough on herself haven't worked, since nobody sees the slips. A flatmate who claims a chore makes each late night cost her at once. A charity count kept alone is easy to let slide.

questions.prompt: A woman kept breaking her promise to send one job application each weekday. Then she and a friend signed a deal: each missed weekday, she buys the friend lunch. From the very first week, she hasn't missed one. What makes it work?
choices: Doing it every single weekday for six weeks turned it into an automatic habit.
Having a friend involved made her care more about getting a job.
Each missed weekday would mean buying a lunch, in front of her friend.
questions.explanation: She kept breaking the same promise before, and the change worked from the first week, before any routine could settle in. What changed is that each skip now costs a lunch, seen by her friend.

reviewCards.front: When a promise to yourself keeps breaking, trying harder alone rarely fixes it. What does fix it is ...
reviewCards.back: ... a written deal with a cost for each slip, signed by someone who will collect it that same day.

reviewCards.front: A man agreed to pay his neighbour $20 for each Monday he didn't post a video to his cooking channel. Six missed Mondays later, she hasn't taken a cent. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: Nobody held him to the deal. Each slip still cost him nothing on the day, so he needs a signer who will actually take the money.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what do you do when you keep breaking a promise to yourself?
reviewCards.back: Write the promise down with a price for each slip, then have someone you care about sign it and collect.

reviewCards.front: For three months you've meant to move $50 into savings on payday, and each time you've spent it instead. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Write a deal with a friend: each payday you skip costs you $10, paid to them that day. Ask them to sign it.

reviewCards.front: Why does a penalty work better when someone else signs the deal than when you set it for yourself?
reviewCards.back: A fine only you know about is easy to let slide. With a signer, each slip costs you right away, in front of someone whose opinion you care about.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Giving every slip a price that someone else holds you to.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I set my alarm on Sunday night for the week ahead, I pick one promise I broke last week, write a cost for each slip, and send it to a friend to sign.
When I notice I've skipped something I promised myself again, I tell one friend that same day and ask them to sign a deal with a cost for the next slip.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, choose the one person whose opinion you care about most. Ask them to sign your deal and to collect the cost on the day you slip.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, go over the days with the person who signed your deal. If a slip went unpaid, pay it right then, and raise the cost for next week.

chapters.title: Pick the Habits Your Body and Nature Are Built For
chapters.hook: You're signing up for the 6 a.m. spin class your fittest friend swears by. Trying twice as hard there may still leave you behind.
chapters.counterintuition: Many people think anyone can get great at any habit if they want it badly enough. Actually, the same effort goes much further in a habit that suits your body and nature, because your genes decide where your odds are best.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Before you commit to a habit, pick one that fits your body and nature, so the odds favor you.
chapters.tryThisNow: Before tonight, set out the one thing you need for whatever makes you lose track of time, and make that your next habit.

memorableLines.text: Choose a habit cut to your shape, and every hour counts for more.
