examples.title: A sister's cold-water swim club
examples.scenario: Hiroko wants a weekly workout. Her older sister swims in a cold lake every Saturday at dawn and keeps texting her the club's sign-up link. Hiroko swims slowly, and cold water makes her shiver just thinking about it. Last Sunday, though, she played badminton with her nephew in the park for two hours and never once checked the time. The link sits open on her phone.
examples.whatToDo: Close the swim link and book a weekly badminton court, since that game already feels like fun and makes the hours vanish.
examples.whyItMatters: The cold swims suit her sister's body and nature. Hiroko's odds are best where hours fly by, so badminton will keep pulling her back.

examples.title: Plant names that won't stick at night
examples.scenario: Zeynep, an apprentice landscaper, must learn three hundred plant names before her spring exam. For three weeks she has forced herself through an hour of textbook every night, coffee at her elbow. She nods off by page two, and on Friday she failed the weekly plant quiz. Out on site, she names every shrub her trainer points at. Still, she feels she isn't cut out for the job.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the nightly textbook hour, tell your trainer it isn't working, and learn the names on site, naming each plant you pass.
examples.whyItMatters: Three weeks of pushing harder at a method that fights her nature cost her a quiz. On site, the same effort already pays her back.

examples.title: Too slow for the staff football game
examples.scenario: Tendai teaches maths at a secondary school. Asked what felt like fun, he chose football and joined the staff game on Thursdays after school. Three weeks in, the younger teachers sprint past him, and he spends most games puffing at the back. He is the tallest player there, with arms that reach almost any high ball. In the car park he tells a colleague, "I'm done. I'm just too slow."
examples.whatToDo: Keep the Thursday game, but ask to play in goal, where your height and long arms let you stand out instead of chasing.
examples.whyItMatters: He can't beat the younger teachers for speed. Being different, not better, turns his build into an edge in the game he enjoys.

questions.prompt: A friend tells you, "I danced for four hours at a street party last night and never checked the clock. Dancing suits me, so tonight I'm signing a year's contract at a salsa school." What is your best reply?
choices: "Sign up tonight, then judge after the full year whether you still love salsa."
"Ask which class your friends enjoyed most, and join that one instead."
"Try a few weeks of salsa and one other dance before you sign."
questions.explanation: Losing track of time at one party is a good sign, but a year is a big promise. A few weeks of salsa and one other dance shows which comes easiest. Judging after the year comes too late.

questions.prompt: Your neighbor wanted a weekly creative habit, so she copied her brother's: oil painting at the kitchen table every Sunday. Painting leaves her restless, yet she happily spends hours writing silly poems for her nieces. When progress stalled, she stayed at the easel an extra hour each week. After two months she quit. Why did the extra effort fail?
choices: She gave herself no treat or reward after each long Sunday at the easel.
She painted at the busy kitchen table, not a quiet room.
She pushed harder at a hobby made for her brother, not her.
questions.explanation: Painting leaves her restless while poems make her hours fly, so the extra hour went into her brother's kind of fun, not hers. A treat afterward would not change how the painting itself felt.

questions.prompt: Your work will pay for one weekly class this year. At a free open day you tried archery, lap swimming and dance fitness. Your closest colleague swims laps every week. Dance fitness left you gasping. In archery the hour vanished, and you hit the target more than the other beginners. Which class do you pick?
choices: Lap swimming, since your closest colleague already goes every week.
Archery, since it already came easier to you than to others.
Dance fitness, since it felt hardest and would stretch you the most.
questions.explanation: In archery the hour vanished and you beat the other beginners, so your odds are best there. Your colleague's swim suits your colleague, and the hardest class is where your effort goes least far.

questions.prompt: A slight, wiry colleague started lifting heavy weights four mornings a week, hoping to look like the bodybuilders at his gym. Two months later he is sore, barely stronger and close to quitting. Which of his three reasons was the trap?
choices: "Training hard enough will give me the same build as theirs."
"I already enjoy the gym far more than most of my friends."
"Mornings are when I have the most energy for training."
questions.explanation: His slight, wiry frame is nothing like the bodybuilders'. Enjoying the gym and training when he has most energy are both sound. Believing hard work alone would give him their build kept him pushing at a poor fit.

questions.prompt: Your friend says, "My brother got fit doing judo, so I'm joining his club for a year. I hate being grabbed, but if I want it enough I'll get used to it." What do you tell her?
choices: "Ask your brother what he loved about judo, and look for that."
"Go to every class anyway, and in time the grabbing will stop bothering you."
"Think about which workouts make the time fly for you, and start there."
questions.explanation: She hates being grabbed, and judo is full of grabbing, so it suits her brother, not her. Asking him still points her at his sport. Starting where time flies for her puts the odds on her side.

questions.prompt: After hard hospital shifts, a nurse tried three ways to unwind: running, a meditation app, then fixing old radios. Radios made hours vanish, and within a month she was fixing sets faster than people with years of practice. A year later she still does it twice a week after shifts. Why has this habit lasted?
choices: Doing it right after shifts gave the habit a fixed time to hang on.
She picked what came naturally to her, so each hour paid her back.
Testing three first built up willpower to stick with the last one.
questions.explanation: Radios made hours vanish and she soon outpaced people with years of practice, so the habit suited her and paid back fast. Running also came after shifts, so the timing alone can't explain it.

questions.prompt: You can lose hours doing silly voices, so you joined a local theatre group. The serious actors there land every big role, and you are starting to dread rehearsals. Yet whenever you play a comic small part, the audience laughs hardest. What is your next move?
choices: Stay, and put your effort into the funny small parts others pass over.
Leave, and test a different hobby where fewer people are this good.
Stay, and ask the group to put on more comedies for you next season.
questions.explanation: Losing hours on voices shows the fit is right, so leaving throws it away. The serious actors win the big roles, but the audience laughs hardest at your comic parts, so be different there.

reviewCards.front: A quiet, private woman forced herself into a loud weekly volleyball league for six months because her friends all play. She still dreads every match and has stopped getting better. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: She picked the habit that suits her friends, not her own nature, then counted on effort to cover the bad fit.

reviewCards.front: In your own words, what should you check before you commit to a new habit?
reviewCards.back: That it suits your body and nature. It should feel like fun to you, make time fly, and come easier to you than to most.

reviewCards.front: Your partner wants you both to start playing squash before work. You're slow on your feet, but you lose hours paddling a kayak on the river. What do you do?
reviewCards.back: Suggest a weekly kayak trip together instead. Squash suits your partner, and paddling is where your body and nature give you the best odds.

reviewCards.front: Why does the same hour of practice take you further in a habit that suits you?
reviewCards.back: Your genes and nature give you a head start there, so each hour builds on strengths instead of fighting weak spots, and the payoff comes sooner.

reviewCards.front: If you can't be better than everyone else at a habit you love, you can still ...
reviewCards.back: ... be different, and find a corner of it where your strengths make you stand out.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Matching each new routine to the build and temperament you already have.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I catch myself thinking I just need to want it more, I ask whether this habit feels like fun to me or only to others.
When I sit down to sign up for a new class, club or app, I first ask whether it makes me lose track of time and whether I do better than most at it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before today ends, write down your answers to the three questions: what feels like fun to you but work to others, what makes you lose track of time, and where you do better than most.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, pick one activity your answers point to and give it a first session. Over the next few weeks, test one or two more for a couple of weeks each, then keep the one that comes easiest.

chapters.title: When a Habit Gets Easy, Make It a Bit Harder
chapters.hook: The workout you finally got good at is the one you'll quit next. It didn't get too hard; it got too easy.
chapters.counterintuition: It feels natural to keep a habit right where it finally got easy. But that comfort is where it starts to die, because people stay hooked on a task only while it is a little past what they can already do.
chapters.keyTakeaway: When a habit starts to feel easy, make it a little harder, just past what you can do now.
chapters.tryThisNow: Tell one person today how you'll make your easiest daily habit one step harder, then do it that way today.

memorableLines.text: Stay at the edge of what you can do, and the habit stays alive.

Aisha has done the morning sudoku on her phone for two months. Now she finishes the easy level before her toast pops, and twice this week she skipped it. She plans to leave it on easy. That plan could cost her the one habit she built this year.

Boredom, not failure, is what kills a habit like hers. James Clear's answer is the Goldilocks Rule: you feel most driven when a task is not too hard and not too easy, but just manageable. In tennis, a small child bores you, a world champion crushes you, and someone at your level keeps you hooked, since you might win. Steve Martin was ten when he got a job at Disneyland, selling guidebooks and later working in the park's magic shop. Later, on stage, he grew his act by just a minute or two a year, keeping the jokes that worked. That steady stretch made him one of the top comedians of his time.

Clear also asks you to show up on dull days, as pros do, but one notch harder is where you can start. So Aisha switches to medium, not expert. Her first puzzle takes twenty minutes, and next morning she can't wait to start. Raise a habit one step past easy whenever it bores you, and you'll want to keep at it.

Aisha has done the morning sudoku on her phone for two months. Now she finishes the easy level before her toast pops, and twice this week she skipped it. She noticed, and she has a plan. She will leave the puzzle on easy and keep the habit just as it is. Building it took real effort, and changing something that works feels like asking for trouble. That plan could cost her the one habit she built this year.

Her thinking makes sense. A new habit is hard at first, and the day it finally feels easy feels like the finish line. But easy has a second side. A task you can do half-asleep gives your mind nothing to hold on to. Soon a morning without it feels no different from a morning with it, and that's when the skipping starts. Boredom, not failure, is what kills a habit like hers.

James Clear calls the answer the Goldilocks Rule, named after the girl in the old children's story who wanted everything just right. You feel most driven when a task is not too hard and not too easy, but just manageable. Too easy, and you get bored. Too hard, and you get discouraged and give up. Right at the edge of what you can do, something better happens. Clear calls it flow, the state of being so wrapped up in a task that the rest of the world fades. It shows up when the challenge sits a bit past what you can already do.

He makes the point with tennis. Play a small child, and you win every point without trying, so you're bored within minutes. Play a world champion, and you lose every point, so you're beaten down just as fast. Now play someone at your own level. Some points you win and some you lose. You might win the match if you try hard, so you stay locked in until the last ball.

Steve Martin's career shows the same idea stretched over many years. He was ten when he got a job at Disneyland, selling guidebooks. Later he worked in the park's magic shop. In time he began performing, and his act grew slowly. Each year he added just a minute or two of new material, and he kept the jokes that worked. He became one of the most successful comedians of his day.

Those small additions are the point. Each year, his act sat only a little past what he could already do. A minute of new jokes was enough to keep him reaching, and not so much that it could crush him. Year after year, the small steps added up.

Clear goes further, asking you to show up on dull days as pros do, but one notch harder is a fine place to begin. When a habit gets too easy, boredom sets in, and that's the moment to act. Don't leave the habit there, and don't leap to the hardest version either, because too hard kills a habit as surely as too easy. Find the next small step, one you can just about manage. It can be a little more, like Steve Martin's extra minute, or a little harder, like a tougher level of the same thing. When that step starts to feel easy too, take the next one.

So Aisha switches the app to medium, not expert. Her first puzzle takes twenty minutes and one wrong guess. She has to think again, and that's what pulls her back. Next morning she can't wait to start. Raise a habit one step past easy whenever it bores you, and you'll want to keep at it.

examples.title: Morning calls that run on autopilot
examples.scenario: For three months, Rahul has started each workday on the sales team at a cleaning company by calling five past clients. They know him, the chats are friendly, and he's done by 9:10. Lately he dials half-asleep and has pushed the calls past lunch twice. This morning his manager drops a list of two hundred offices nobody has called onto his desk.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the five friendly calls, and add one call a day from the new list, to a stranger who might say no.
examples.whyItMatters: Five warm calls no longer stretch him, and two hundred cold ones would crush him. One new call keeps his mornings just manageable.

examples.title: A cello piece far out of reach
examples.scenario: Gideon played the same three beginner cello pieces for months. Bored, he asked his teacher for the hardest piece in her book. That was three weeks ago. He still can't get through the first line, the page is gray with pencil marks, and he has stopped practicing. His Thursday lesson is tomorrow, and he dreads it.
examples.whatToDo: Tell his teacher the leap was too big, put the hard piece away, and ask for one just a step past his three easy ones.
examples.whyItMatters: Too hard crushed him just as too easy bored him. A piece he can just about play brings back the pull to practice.

examples.title: Twenty minutes in the park before the trains
examples.scenario: Every Tuesday at seven, Ugo and two friends kick a football around the park for twenty minutes before their trains. At first the passing drills had them laughing and swearing. Now they pass on autopilot, talking about work. None of them can stay a minute past 7:20, and last week one friend said, "Maybe we just get coffee instead."
examples.whatToDo: Keep the twenty minutes, but make one drill harder, like passing only with the weaker foot for the last five minutes.
examples.whyItMatters: They can't add time, so the step has to be harder, not longer. One tougher drill puts the morning just past what they can do.

questions.prompt: For four months, a man has cooked one of the same three dinners every weeknight, whenever he gets home, to keep his new habit safe. He no longer needs the recipes. Now he orders takeaway most nights, though his evenings are no busier. Why did keeping it safe backfire?
choices: The dinners no longer stretched him, so cooking slowly stopped holding his interest.
He never set a fixed time for cooking, so the plan drifted.
Cooking dinner on every single weeknight was too big a goal to start with.
questions.explanation: He cooked the same three dinners for four months and no longer needs the recipes, so they stopped stretching him and boredom set in. A goal he kept up for four months was not too big.

questions.prompt: You've knitted one plain scarf a month for half a year. You finished the last one during a film, hardly looking down. What do you knit next?
choices: Another plain scarf, since the routine is finally running smoothly.
A sweater with cables all over, the hardest pattern in the shop.
A scarf that uses one simple stitch you've never tried before.
questions.explanation: You knitted the last scarf hardly looking, so plain scarves no longer stretch you. One new stitch is just past what you can do, while a sweater covered in cables would crush you.

questions.prompt: A woman has folded one paper crane each evening for two months, about ten minutes' work. Now she folds it during the TV news without looking, and she has skipped three evenings. She sticks with cranes, telling herself three things, and a month later she has quit. Which of her three reasons was the trap?
choices: Folding just one crane every single evening is what keeps it going.
Ten minutes is short enough to fit into any evening.
Cranes take no effort now, so the tough part is over.
questions.explanation: Folding every evening and keeping it short are both sound. The trap was treating ease as the finish line: she folds during the news without looking, so cranes stopped holding her, and boredom made her quit.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I can now chat in my Korean class without notes. The class drags lately, but I never miss, so I'm staying with the beginners." What is your best reply?
choices: "Stay with the beginners, but add a second class every single week."
"Try the next group up, where you still trip up sometimes."
"Write down why you're learning Korean so you keep going."
questions.explanation: Chatting without notes means the beginner class no longer stretches your friend, which is why it drags. They never miss, so written reasons won't help, and a second beginner class only adds more of the same.

questions.prompt: A woman paddled the same calm stretch of river every Sunday for a year, and it grew dull. Now she paddles that stretch upstream, against a gentle current, past the same views. She looks forward to Sundays again. Why did the change work?
choices: Going upstream made each trip seem new, and the change itself kept her keen.
Paddling upstream stretched her, but the trip still stayed within her reach.
Going upstream was so tough that just finishing it was a big win.
questions.explanation: The current is gentle, so the trip tests her without beating her. The views haven't changed, so it was the stretch, not anything new to look at, that brought back the pull to paddle.

questions.prompt: A man has sung in a community choir for two years. The songs are easy now, and he yawns through Tuesday rehearsals. The only other choir nearby sings opera, far past his level. What is his best move?
choices: Ask to learn the trickier harmony line in the choir he's in.
Audition for the opera choir and learn the hard pieces as he goes.
Take a few weeks off choir so the old songs seem fresh.
questions.explanation: Opera is far past his level and would crush him, and a break leaves the old songs just as easy. A trickier harmony line in his own choir is one step past what he can sing now.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "Last year I moved up from 500-piece jigsaws to 1,000-piece ones. Now I finish those in an evening without trying, but I've already moved up once." What do you say back?
choices: "Then you've done the work, so just enjoy the 1,000-piece ones."
"Moving up was right, and now that they're quick, move up again."
"Try a whole new hobby instead, since jigsaws have likely run their course."
questions.explanation: Your friend moved up once, but the 1,000-piece puzzles now take no effort, so they're back to too easy. The missing part is moving up again, and a new hobby throws away a habit that only needs stretching.

reviewCards.front: You can sing every song on your karaoke list without missing a word, and karaoke nights have started to feel flat. What's your move?
reviewCards.back: Add one song that's a bit beyond your range or speed, not the hardest one going, so the night holds you again.

reviewCards.front: Why does a habit you've finally mastered start to slip away?
reviewCards.back: Once it's too easy, it bores you, and boredom, not failure, is what makes people drift off. A small new challenge pulls you back in.

reviewCards.front: When a habit gets easy, the next step should be just big enough to ...
reviewCards.back: ... stretch you a bit past what you can do now, but not so big that it crushes you.

reviewCards.front: Bored with hitting the near target at archery club, a man moved straight to the farthest one, missed every arrow for a week, and quit. What went wrong?
reviewCards.back: He jumped too far. Too hard crushes a habit as surely as too easy bores it. A target one step farther would have kept him coming back.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting when a routine has stopped stretching you, and raising it by one small notch.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I notice I'm doing a habit on autopilot or putting it off, I make it one small step harder the next time I do it.
When I finish the last task of my work week, I pick one habit that felt easy this week and choose its next small step.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Before tonight, pick one thing you do every day that now runs on autopilot, and do it once at a slightly harder level.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, list your habits and mark any that felt easy or dull. For each one, set a small next step, like a minute more or a slightly harder level, never the hardest.

chapters.title: Why Daily Habits Stall, and How to Keep Getting Better
chapters.hook: You've driven every day for ten years, yet you still need three tries to park. How can that much practice stop making you better?
chapters.counterintuition: You have probably been told that doing a habit every day keeps making you better. The trouble is that once it runs on its own, you stop noticing small mistakes, so you need to pick one part and practice it on purpose.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Once a habit runs on its own, pick one small part of it and practice that part on purpose.
chapters.tryThisNow: Write on a scrap of paper the one part of a daily habit that still goes wrong, and leave it where you do that habit.

memorableLines.text: Autopilot keeps a habit going; working one weak piece on purpose makes it better.

breakdown.fastRead:
How can someone practice every day for years and still stop improving? James Clear says the habit itself is the cause. Once it runs on its own, you stop watching closely, and small mistakes slip past. Getting really good takes habits plus practice on purpose, which means hard work on one small part you are weak at.

Clear shows this with the Los Angeles Lakers basketball team. After the team lost in the 1986 playoffs, their coach, Pat Riley, started a program called Career Best Effort. He tracked each player's numbers against a baseline score and asked each one to improve on it by at least 1 percent over the season. Now skilled players had to look hard at each part of their game. About eight months later, the Lakers won the championship.

The usual answer to feeling stuck is to push harder and do more. But more hours on autopilot just repeat the same mistakes. Clear pairs this practice on purpose with a review of your progress on a set schedule, a yearly review in his case. If you still need three tries to park, practice only backing into spaces, slowly. Once that runs on its own, it becomes the ground for the next part. When you pick one small part of a habit that runs itself and practice it on purpose, you start getting better again.

examples.title: Two years of Thursdays in the choir
examples.scenario: Kwabena has sung tenor in his neighbourhood choir every Thursday for two years. He knows every song by heart now and barely thinks while singing. Yet last week's recording sounded just like one from a year ago, with the same wobble on the long high notes. Tonight, sheet music in hand at the church hall, he wonders how to spend the warm-up.
examples.whatToDo: Spend the warm-up on just the long high notes, singing each one slowly and listening for the wobble, instead of running whole songs.
examples.whyItMatters: Singing on autopilot let the wobble slip by for two years. Working only on those notes makes him hear it again.

examples.title: An extra hour of latte hearts
examples.scenario: Marisol has made lattes at a corner cafe for three years, and her milk hearts still come out lopsided. Last month she made a strict rule: stay an hour after every shift and pour drink after drink. Now she is worn out, the owner has noticed the milk bill doubling, and the hearts look the same as before.
examples.whatToDo: Drop the extra hour and own up to the owner about the milk. Then spend five slow minutes each morning on only the last tilt of the jug.
examples.whyItMatters: An hour of pouring on autopilot just repeated the same lopsided pour. Working one small part makes her watch the step that goes wrong.

examples.title: The word that shut the book
examples.scenario: Bilal listens to his daughter Renata read aloud on the back steps after school, for her reading log. She reads fast and smoothly now, but she guesses at long words instead of sounding them out. When he stopped her on "enormous" yesterday, she slammed the book shut. "I'm the best reader in my class," she said, cheeks red.
examples.whatToDo: Shrink the practice to one long word a night, picked together before she starts, and let her read the rest of the page her own way.
examples.whyItMatters: Her pride can take one word. Once sounding out that kind of word runs on its own, it becomes the ground for the next.

questions.prompt: You've played darts in a league at your local social club every week for two years. Your throws feel automatic, your scores haven't moved, and most misses land low and left. A video you saved covers stance, grip and release. What do you do?
choices: Spend each warm-up working on your stance, grip and release all together.
Spend each warm-up throwing only to fix your usual low-left miss.
Spend each warm-up on the throws you already land well.
questions.explanation: Your misses keep landing low and left, so that is the weak part. Warming up only on it makes you notice the small mistake again. Stance, grip and release all together spreads your attention over everything at once.

questions.prompt: Anand has phoned his in-laws every Sunday for two years to practice his Portuguese. The talk now flows without pauses, yet he still mixes up the same past-tense endings he did at the start. He gives three reasons for keeping the calls just as they are. Which one do these facts show is false?
choices: Talking with them each week still makes me a bit better.
Calling at the same time each week makes starting easy.
These days I can chat with them without stopping to think.
questions.explanation: Two years of calls left the same endings wrong, so talking each week was not making him better. The other two are true: a set time makes starting easy, and chatting without stopping to think shows the habit now runs on its own, which is also why the mistakes slip by.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "I've played golf every Saturday for five years without missing one. My putting is still shaky, but I'll keep playing my rounds and it'll come." What is your best reply?
choices: "Spend half an hour before each round on putting and nothing else."
"Set yourself a firm deadline to fix your putting by summer."
"Keep at it, since five more years of rounds will smooth it out."
questions.explanation: Five years of rounds left the putting shaky, so more rounds will just repeat it. Half an hour on putting alone makes your friend watch the small mistakes. A deadline adds pressure but changes nothing about how they putt.

questions.prompt: Luca has given the same welcome talk to castle tour groups every day for two years, and guests always drifted off at the same point. He began recording one talk a week and working only on that stretch. A month later, guests stay with him to the end. Why did this work?
choices: Hearing himself on the recordings gave him more confidence with each group.
Two years of daily talks had finally built enough skill.
Working on that one stretch let him catch slips he'd missed.
questions.explanation: Guests drifted off at the same point for two years, so daily talks alone weren't helping. Working only on that stretch made him notice slips he had stopped catching. More confidence would not explain one spot changing.

questions.prompt: You've bowled in a Tuesday league for years. Every frame feels smooth and automatic, your average hasn't moved all season, and you honestly can't tell which part of your game is weak. Like Riley's players, you want a starting mark of your own to beat. What should come first?
choices: Track your strikes and spares for a month, then work the weaker.
Start working on your spares right away, since most bowlers find those hardest.
Work a little on every shot, since none stands out.
questions.explanation: You can't tell which part is weak, so a guess may pick the wrong one. Riley tracked each player's numbers against a baseline so each knew what to push on, and Clear pairs practice on purpose with a regular review of how you are doing. Tracking strikes and spares does the same and shows which part to work on.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "For a month I worked only on writing shorter summaries in my weekly reports. Now I do it without thinking, so my report writing is sorted." What do you tell them?
choices: "Keep drilling the summaries another month so they really stick."
"Now pick the next weak spot in your reports and drill that."
"Teach the new summary style to your whole team so they improve too."
questions.explanation: The summaries now run on their own, so they are ground to stand on. What's missing is the next weak spot in the reports. Another month on summaries repeats a part that is already done.

questions.prompt: A bricklayer's apprentice has laid bricks every workday for a year, but her walls still lean slightly at the corners. Her boss made her lay twice as many bricks a day. A month on, the corners lean exactly as before. Why didn't doubling the work help?
choices: One month was too short for the extra bricks to pay off.
Twice the bricks left her too tired to work carefully.
More bricks laid the usual way just repeated the corner mistake.
questions.explanation: A year of daily bricklaying hadn't fixed the corners, so more of the same couldn't either. Laid the usual way, each extra brick repeated the mistake. Tiredness doesn't explain corners leaning exactly as before.

reviewCards.back: Spend a few minutes each evening knitting only the edge stitches, slowly and carefully, until they come out even.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Spotting the weak piece of something you already do without thinking, and giving that piece your full attention.

ifThenPlans.plan: When I sit down to a task I've done the same way for months, I spend the first five minutes on the one small part I'm weakest at.
When I catch myself thinking that doing it daily is enough to improve, I write down the one part that still goes wrong and work only on it next time.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next day, spend five minutes on the part you wrote down, doing only that part slowly and watching for the mistake.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, check whether the part you chose now runs without thought. If it does, pick the next weak part of the same habit and give it the same five minutes.
